What these horrible creatures - and Charles Ward as well - were doing or trying to do seemed fairly clear from their letters and from every bit of light both old and new which had filtered in upon the case. They were robbing the tombs of all the ages
column7: including those of the world's wisest and greatest men
column8: in the hope of recovering from the bygone ashes some vestige of the consciousness and lore which had once animated and informed them.

column1: A hideous traffick was going on among these nightmare ghouls
column2: whereby illustrious bones were bartered with the calm calculativeness of schoolboys swapping books; and from what was extorted from this centuried dust there was anticipated a power and a wisdom beyond anything which the cosmos had ever seen concentrated in one man or group. They had found unholy ways to keep their brains alive
column3: either in the same body or different bodies; and had evidently achieved a way of tapping the consciousness of the dead whom they gathered together. There had
column4: it seems
column5: been some truth in chimerical old Borellus when he wrote of preparing from even the most antique remains certain ""Essential Saltes"" from which the shade of a long-dead living thing might be raised up. There was a formula for evoking such a shade
column6: and another for putting it down; and it had now been so perfected that it could be taught successfully. One must be careful about evocations
column7: for the markers of old graves are not always accurate.

column1: Willett and Mr. Ward shivered as they passed from conclusion to conclusion. Things - presences or voices of some sort - could be drawn down from unknown places as well as from the grave
column2: and in this process also one must be careful. Joseph Curwen had indubitably evoked many forbidden things
column3: and as for Charles - what might one think of him? What forces ""outside the spheres"" had reached him from Joseph Curwen's day and turned his mind on forgotten things? He had been led to find certain directions
column4: and he had used them. He had talked with the man of horror in Prague and stayed long with the creature in the mountains of Transylvania. And he must have found the grave of Joseph Curwen at last. That newspaper item and what his mother had heard in the night were too significant to overlook. Then he had summoned something
column5: and it must have come. That mighty voice aloft on Good Friday
column6: and those different tones in the locked attic laboratory. What were they like
column7: with their depth and hollowness? Was there not here some awful foreshadowing of the dreaded stranger Dr. Allen with his spectral bass? Yes
column8: that was what Mr. Ward had felt with vague horror in his single talk with the man - if man it were - over the telephone!

column1: What hellish consciousness or voice
column3: had come to answer Charles Ward's secret rites behind that locked door? Those voices heard in argument - ""must have it red for three months"" - Good God! Was not that just before the vampirism broke out? The rifling of Ezra Weeden's ancient grave
column4: and the cries later at Pawtuxet - whose mind had planned the vengeance and rediscovered the shunned seat of elder blasphemies? And then the bungalow and the bearded stranger
column5: and the gossip
column6: and the fear. The final madness of Charles neither father nor doctor could attempt to explain
column7: but they did feel sure that the mind of Joseph Curwen had come to earth again and was following its ancient morbidities. Was daemoniac possession in truth a possibility? Allen had something to do with it
column8: and the detectives must find out more about one whose existence menaced the young man's life. In the meantime
column9: since the existence of some vast crypt beneath the bungalow seemed virtually beyond dispute
column10: some effort must be made to find it. Willett and Mr. Ward
column11: conscious of the sceptical attitude of the alienists
column12: resolved during their final conference to undertake a joint secret exploration of unparalleled thoroughness; and agreed to meet at the bungalow on the following morning with valises and with certain tools and accessories suited to architectural search and underground exploration.

column1: The morning of April 6th dawned clear
column2: and both explorers were at the bungalow by ten o'clock. Mr. Ward had the key
column3: and an entry and cursory survey were made. From the disordered condition of Dr. Allen's room it was obvious that the detectives had been there before
column4: and the later searchers hoped that they had found some clue which might prove of value. Of course the main business lay in the cellar; so thither they descended without much delay
column5: again making the circuit which each had vainly made before in the presence of the mad young owner. For a time everything seemed baffling
column6: each inch of the earthen floor and stone walls having so solid and innocuous an aspect that the thought of a yawning aperture was scarcely to be entertained. Willett reflected that since the original cellar was dug without knowledge of any catacombs beneath
column7: the beginning of the passage would represent the strictly modern delving of young Ward and his associates
column8: where they had probed for the ancient vaults whose rumour could have reached them by no wholesome means.

column1: The doctor tried to put himself in Charles's place to see how a delver would be likely to start
column2: but could not gain much inspiration from this method. Then he decided on elimination as a policy
column3: and went carefully over the whole subterranean surface both vertical and horizontal
column4: trying to account for every inch separately. He was soon substantially narrowed down
column5: and at last had nothing left but the small platform before the washtubs
column6: which he had tried once before in vain. Now experimenting in every possible way
column7: and exerting a double strength
column8: he finally found that the top did indeed turn and slide horizontally on a corner pivot. Beneath it lay a trim concrete surface with an iron manhole
column9: to which Mr. Ward at once rushed with excited zeal. The cover was not hard to lift
column10: and the father had quite removed it when Willett noticed the queerness of his aspect. He was swaying and nodding dizzily
column11: and in the gust of noxious air which swept up from the black pit beneath the doctor soon recognised ample cause.

column1: In a moment Dr. Willett had his fainting companion on the floor above and was reviving him with cold water. Mr. Ward responded feebly
column2: but it could be seen that the mephitic blast from the crypt had in some way gravely sickened him. Wishing to take no chances
column3: Willett hastened out to Broad Street for a taxicab and had soon dispatched the sufferer home despite his weak-voiced protests; after which he produced an electric torch
column4: covered his nostrils with a band of sterile gauze
column5: and descended once more to peer into the new-found depths. The foul air had now slightly abated
column6: and Willett was able to send a beam of light down the Stygian hole. For about ten feet
column7: he saw
column8: it was a sheer cylindrical drop with concrete walls and an iron ladder; after which the hole appeared to strike a flight of old stone steps which must originally have emerged to earth somewhat southwest of the present building.

column1: Willett freely admits that for a moment the memory of the old Curwen legends kept him from climbing down alone into that malodorous gulf. He could not help thinking of what Luke Fenner had reported on that last monstrous night. Then duty asserted itself and he made the plunge
column2: carrying a great valise for the removal of whatever papers might prove of supreme importance. Slowly
column3: as befitted one of his years
column4: he descended the ladder and reached the slimy steps below. This was ancient masonry
column5: his torch told him; and upon the dripping walls he saw the unwholesome moss of centuries. Down
column6: down
column7: ran the steps; not spirally
column8: but in three abrupt turns; and with such narrowness that two men could have passed only with difficulty. He had counted about thirty when a sound reached him very faintly; and after that he did not feel disposed to count any more.

column1: It was a godless sound; one of those low-keyed
column2: insidious outrages of Nature which are not meant to be. To call it a dull wail
column3: a doom-dragged whine
column4: or a hopeless howl of chorused anguish and stricken flesh without mind would be to miss its most quintessential loathsomeness and soul-sickening overtones. Was it for this that Ward had seemed to listen on that day he was removed? It was the most shocking thing that Willett had ever heard
column5: and it continued from no determinate point as the doctor reached the bottom of the steps and cast his torchlight around on lofty corridor walls surmounted by Cyclopean vaulting and pierced by numberless black archways. The hall in which he stood was perhaps fourteen feet high to the middle of the vaulting and ten or twelve feet broad. Its pavement was of large chipped flagstones
column6: and its walls and roof were of dressed masonry. Its length he could not imagine
column7: for it stretched ahead indefinitely into the blackness. Of the archways
column8: some had doors of the old six-panelled colonial type
column9: whilst others had none.

column1: Overcoming the dread induced by the smell and the howling
column2: Willett began to explore these archways one by one; finding beyond them rooms with groined stone ceilings
column3: each of medium size and apparently of bizarre uses. Most of them had fireplaces
column4: the upper courses of whose chimneys would have formed an interesting study in engineering. Never before or since had he seen such instruments or suggestions of instruments as here loomed up on every hand through the burying dust and cobwebs of a century and a half
column5: in many cases evidently shattered as if by the ancient raiders. For many of the chambers seemed wholly untrodden by modern feet
column6: and must have represented the earliest and most obsolete phases of Joseph Curwen's experimentation. Finally there came a room of obvious modernity
column7: or at least of recent occupancy. There were oil heaters
column8: bookshelves and tables
column9: chairs and cabinets
column10: and a desk piled high with papers of varying antiquity and contemporaneousness. Candlesticks and oil lamps stood about in several places; and finding a match-safe handy
column11: Willett lighted such as were ready for use.

column1: In the fuller gleam it appeared that this apartment was nothing less than the latest study or library of Charles Ward. Of the books the doctor had seen many before
column2: and a good part of the furniture had plainly come from the Prospect Street mansion. Here and there was a piece well known to Willett
column3: and the sense of familiarity became so great that he half forgot the noisomeness and the wailing
column4: both of which were plainer here than they had been at the foot of the steps. His first duty
column5: as planned long ahead
column6: was to find and seize any papers which might seem of vital importance; especially those portentous documents found by Charles so long ago behind the picture in Olney Court. As he searched he perceived how stupendous a task the final unravelling would be; for file on file was stuffed with papers in curious hands and bearing curious designs
column7: so that months or even years might be needed for a thorough deciphering and editing. Once he found large packets of letters with Prague and Rakus postmarks
column8: and in writing clearly recognisable as Orne's and Hutchinson's; all of which he took with him as part of the bundle to be removed in his valise.

column1: At last
column2: in a locked mahogany cabinet once gracing the Ward home
column3: Willett found the batch of old Curwen papers; recognising them from the reluctant glimpse Charles had granted him so many years ago. The youth had evidently kept them together very much as they had been when first he found them
column4: since all the titles recalled by the workmen were present except the papers addressed to Orne and Hutchinson
column5: and the cipher with its key. Willett placed the entire lot in his valise and continued his examination of the files. Since young Ward's immediate condition was the greatest matter at stake
column6: the closest searching was done among the most obviously recent matter; and in this abundance of contemporary manuscript one very baffling oddity was noted. The oddity was the slight amount in Charles's normal writing
column7: which indeed included nothing more recent than two months before. On the other hand
column8: there were literally reams of symbols and formulae
column9: historical notes and philosophical comment
column10: in a crabbed penmanship absolutely identical with the ancient script of Joseph Curwen
column11: though of undeniably modern dating. Plainly
column12: a part of the latter-day programme had been a sedulous imitation of the old wizard's writing
column13: which Charles seemed to have carried to a marvellous state of perfection. Of any third hand which might have been Allen's there was not a trace. If he had indeed come to be the leader
column14: he must have forced young Ward to act as his amanuensis.

column1: In this new material one mystic formula
column3: recurred so often that Willett had it by heart before he had half finished his quest. It consisted of two parallel columns
column4: the left-hand one surmounted by the archaic symbol called ""Dragon's Head"" and used in almanacks to indicate the ascending node
column5: and the right-hand one headed by a corresponding sign of ""Dragon's Tail"" or descending node. The appearance of the whole was something like this
column6: and almost unconsciously the doctor realised that the second half was no more than the first written syllabically backward with the exception of the final monosyllables and of the odd name Yog-Sothoth
column7: which he had come to recognise under various spellings from other things he had seen in connexion with this horrible matter. The formulae were as follows - exactly so
column8: as Willett is abundantly able to testify - and the first one struck an odd note of uncomfortable latent memory in his brain
column9: which he recognised later when reviewing the events of that horrible Good Friday of the previous year.

column1: Y'AI 'NG'NGAH
YOG-SOTHOTH
H'EE - L'GEB
F'AI THRODOG
UAAAH
OGTHROD AI'F
GEB'L - EE'H
YOG-SOTHOTH
'NGAH'NG AI'Y
ZHRO
So haunting were these formulae
column2: and so frequently did he come upon them
column3: that before the doctor knew it he was repeating them under his breath. Eventually
column4: however
column5: he felt he had secured all the papers he could digest to advantage for the present; hence resolved to examine no more till he could bring the sceptical alienists en masse for an ampler and more systematic raid. He had still to find the hidden laboratory
column6: so leaving his valise in the lighted room he emerged again into the black noisome corridor whose vaulting echoed ceaselessly with that dull and hideous whine.

column1: The next few rooms he tried were all abandoned
column2: or filled only with crumbling boxes and ominous-looking leaden coffins; but impressed him deeply with the magnitude of Joseph Curwen's original operations. He thought of the slaves and seamen who had disappeared
column3: of the graves which had been violated in every part of the world
column4: and of what that final raiding party must have seen; and then he decided it was better not to think any more. Once a great stone staircase mounted at his right
column5: and he deduced that this must have reached to one of the Curwen outbuildings - perhaps the famous stone edifice with the high slit-like windows - provided the steps he had descended had led from the steep-roofed farmhouse. Suddenly the walls seemed to fall away ahead
column6: and the stench and the wailing grew stronger. Willett saw that he had come upon a vast open space
column7: so great that his torchlight would not carry across it; and as he advanced he encountered occasional stout pillars supporting the arches of the roof.

column1: After a time he reached a circle of pillars grouped like the monoliths of Stonehenge
column2: with a large carved altar on a base of three steps in the centre; and so curious were the carvings on that altar that he approached to study them with his electric light. But when he saw what they were he shrank away shuddering
column3: and did not stop to investigate the dark stains which discoloured the upper surface and had spread down the sides in occasional thin lines. Instead
column4: he found the distant wall and traced it as it swept round in a gigantic circle perforated by occasional black doorways and indented by a myriad of shallow cells with iron gratings and wrist and ankle bonds on chains fastened to the stone of the concave rear masonry. These cells were empty
column5: but still the horrible odour and the dismal moaning continued
column6: more insistent now than ever
column7: and seemingly varied at times by a sort of slippery thumping.

column1: From that frightful smell and that uncanny noise Willett's attention could no longer be diverted. Both were plainer and more hideous in the great pillared hall than anywhere else
column2: and carried a vague impression of being far below
column3: even in this dark nether world of subterrene mystery. Before trying any of the black archways for steps leading further down
column4: the doctor cast his beam of light about the stone-flagged floor. It was very loosely paved
column5: and at irregular intervals there would occur a slab curiously pierced by small holes in no definite arrangement
column6: while at one point there lay a very long ladder carelessly flung down. To this ladder
column7: singularly enough
column8: appeared to cling a particularly large amount of the frightful odour which encompassed everything. As he walked slowly about it suddenly occurred to Willett that both the noise and the odour seemed strongest directly above the oddly pierced slabs
column9: as if they might be crude trap-doors leading down to some still deeper region of horror. Kneeling by one
column10: he worked at it with his hands
column11: and found that with extreme difficulty he could budge it. At his touch the moaning beneath ascended to a louder key
column12: and only with vast trepidation did he persevere in the lifting of the heavy stone. A stench unnamable now rose up from below
column13: and the doctor's head reeled dizzily as he laid back the slab and turned his torch upon the exposed square yard of gaping blackness.

column1: If he had expected a flight of steps to some wide gulf of ultimate abomination
column2: Willett was destined to be disappointed; for amidst that foetor and cracked whining he discerned only the brick-faced top of a cylindrical well perhaps a yard and a half in diameter and devoid of any ladder or other means of descent. As the light shone down
column3: the wailing changed suddenly to a series of horrible yelps; in conjunction with which there came again that sound of blind
column4: futile scrambling and slippery thumping. The explorer trembled
column5: unwilling even to imagine what noxious thing might be lurking in that abyss
column6: but in a moment mustered up the courage to peer over the rough-hewn brink; lying at full length and holding the torch downward at arm's length to see what might lie below. For a second he could distinguish nothing but the slimy
column7: moss-grown brick walls sinking illimitably into that half-tangible miasma of murk and foulness and anguished frenzy; and then he saw that something dark was leaping clumsily and frantically up and down at the bottom of the narrow shaft
column8: which must have been from twenty to twenty-five feet below the stone floor where he lay. The torch shook in his hand
column9: but he looked again to see what manner of living creature might be immured there in the darkness of that unnatural well; left starving by young Ward through all the long month since the doctors had taken him away
column10: and clearly only one of a vast number prisoned in the kindred wells whose pierced stone covers so thickly studded in the floor of the great vaulted cavern. Whatever the things were
column11: they could not lie down in their cramped spaces; but must have crouched and whined and waited and feebly leaped all those hideous weeks since their master had abandoned them unheeded.

column1: But Marinus Bicknell Willett was sorry that he looked again; for surgeon and veteran of the dissecting-room though he was
column2: he has not been the same since. It is hard to explain just how a single sight of a tangible object with measureable dimensions could so shake and change a man; and we may only say that there is about certain outlines and entities a power of symbolism and suggestion which acts frightfully on a sensitive thinker's perspective and whispers terrible hints of obscure cosmic relationships and unnamable realities behind the protective illusions of common vision. In that second look Willett saw such an outline or entity
column3: for during the next few instants he was undoubtedly as stark mad as any inmate of Dr. Waite's private hospital. He dropped the electric torch from a hand drained of muscular power or nervous cordination
column4: nor heeded the sound of crunching teeth which told of its fate at the bottom of the pit. He screamed and screamed and screamed in a voice whose falsetto panic no acquaintance of his would ever have recognised; and though he could not rise to his feet he crawled and rolled desperately away over the damp pavement where dozens of Tartarean wells poured forth their exhausted whining and yelping to answer his own insane cries. He tore his hands on the rough
column5: loose stones
column6: and many times bruised his head against the frequent pillars
column7: but still he kept on. Then at last he slowly came to himself in the utter blackness and stench
column8: and stopped his ears against the droning wail into which the burst of yelping had subsided. He was drenched with perspiration and without means of producing a light; stricken and unnerved in the abysmal blackness and horror
column9: and crushed with a memory he never could efface. Beneath him dozens of those things still lived
column10: and from one of the shafts the cover was removed. He knew that what he had seen could never climb up the slippery walls
column11: yet shuddered at the thought that some obscure foot-hold might exist.

column1: What the thing was
column2: he would never tell. It was like some of the carvings on the hellish altar
column3: but it was alive. Nature had never made it in this form
column4: for it was too palpably unfinished. The deficiencies were of the most surprising sort
column5: and the abnormalities of proportion could not be described. Willett consents only to say that this type of thing must have represented entities which Ward called up from imperfect salts
column6: and which he kept for servile or ritualistic purposes. If it had not had a certain significance
column7: its image would not have been carved on that damnable stone. It was not the worst thing depicted on that stone - but Willett never opened the other pits. At the time
column8: the first connected idea in his mind was an idle paragraph from some of the old Curwen data he had digested long before; a phrase used by Simon or Jedediah Orne in that portentous confiscated letter to the bygone sorcerer: ""Certainely
column9: there was Noth'g butt ye liveliest Awfulness in that which H. rais'd upp from What he cou'd gather onlie a part of.""

column1: Then
column2: horribly supplementing rather than displacing this image
column3: there came a recollection of those ancient lingering rumours anent the burned
column4: twisted thing found in the fields a week after the Curwen raid. Charles Ward had once told the doctor what old Slocum said of that object; that it was neither thoroughly human
column5: nor wholly allied to any animal which Pawtuxet folk had ever seen or read about.

column1: These words hummed in the doctor's mind as he rocked to and fro
column2: squatting on the nitrous stone floor. He tried to drive them out
column3: and repeated the Lord's Prayer to himself; eventually trailing off into a mnemonic hodge-podge like the modernistic Waste Land of Mr. T. S. Eliot and finally reverting to the oft-repeated dual formula he had lately found in Ward's underground library: ""Y'ai 'ng'ngah
column4: Yog-Sothoth""
column5: and so on till the final underlined ""Zhro"". It seemed to soothe him
column6: and he staggered to his feet after a time; lamenting bitterly his fright-lost torch and looking wildly about for any gleam of light in the clutching inkiness of the chilly air. Think he would not; but he strained his eyes in every direction for some faint glint or reflection of the bright illumination he had left in the library. After a while he thought he detected a suspicion of a glow infinitely far away
column7: and toward this he crawled in agonised caution on hands and knees amidst the stench and howling
column8: always feeling ahead lest he collide with the numerous great pillars or stumble into the abominable pit he had uncovered.

column1: Once his shaking fingers touched something which he knew must be the steps leading to the hellish altar
column2: and from this spot he recoiled in loathing. At another time he encountered the pierced slab he had removed
column3: and here his caution became almost pitiful. But he did not come upon the dread aperture after all
column4: nor did anything issue from that aperture to detain him. What had been down there made no sound nor stir. Evidently its crunching of the fallen electric torch had not been good for it. Each time Willett's fingers felt a perforated slab he trembled. His passage over it would sometimes increase the groaning below
column5: but generally it would produce no effect at all
column6: since he moved very noiselessly. Several times during his progress the glow ahead diminished perceptibly
column7: and he realised that the various candles and lamps he had left must be expiring one by one. The thought of being lost in utter darkness without matches amidst this underground world of nightmare labyrinths impelled him to rise to his feet and run
column8: which he could safely do now that he had passed the open pit; for he knew that once the light failed
column9: his only hope of rescue and survival would lie in whatever relief party Mr. Ward might send after missing him for a sufficient period. Presently
column10: however
column11: he emerged from the open space into the narrower corridor and definitely located the glow as coming from a door on his right. In a moment he had reached it and was standing once more in young Ward's secret library
column12: trembling with relief
column13: and watching the sputterings of that last lamp which had brought him to safety.

column1: In another moment he was hastily filling the burned-out lamps from an oil supply he had previously noticed
column2: and when the room was bright again he looked about to see if he might find a lantern for further exploration. For racked though he was with horror
column3: his sense of grim purpose was still uppermost; and he was firmly determined to leave no stone unturned in his search for the hideous facts behind Charles Ward's bizarre madness. Failing to find a lantern
column4: he chose the smallest of the lamps to carry; also filling his pockets with candles and matches
column5: and taking with him a gallon can of oil
column6: which he proposed to keep for reserve use in whatever hidden laboratory he might uncover beyond the terrible open space with its unclean altar and nameless covered wells. To traverse that space again would require his utmost fortitude
column7: but he knew it must be done. Fortunately neither the frightful altar nor the opened shaft was near the vast cell-indented wall which bounded the cavern area
column8: and whose black mysterious archways would form the next goals of a logical search.

column1: So Willett went back to that great pillared hall of stench and anguished howling; turning down his lamp to avoid any distant glimpse of the hellish altar
column2: or of the uncovered pit with the pierced stone slab beside it. Most of the black doorways led merely to small chambers
column3: some vacant and some evidently used as storerooms; and in several of the latter he saw some very curious accumulations of various objects. One was packed with rotting and dust-draped bales of spare clothing
column4: and the explorer thrilled when he saw that it was unmistakably the clothing of a century and a half before. In another room he found numerous odds and ends of modern clothing
column5: as if gradual provisions were being made to equip a large body of men. But what he disliked most of all were the huge copper vats which occasionally appeared; these
column6: and the sinister incrustations upon them. He liked them even less than the weirdly figured leaden bowls whose rims retained such obnoxious deposits and around which clung repellent odours perceptible above even the general noisomeness of the crypt. When he had completed about half the entire circuit of the wall he found another corridor like that from which he had come
column7: and out of which many doors opened. This he proceeded to investigate; and after entering three rooms of medium size and of no significant contents
column8: he came at last to a large oblong apartment whose business-like tanks and tables
column9: furnaces and modern instruments
column10: occasional books and endless shelves of jars and bottles proclaimed it indeed the long-sought laboratory of Charles Ward - and no doubt of old Joseph Curwen before him.

column1: After lighting the three lamps which he found filled and ready
column2: Dr. Willett examined the place and all its appurtenances with the keenest interest; noting from the relative quantities of various reagents on the shelves that young Ward's dominant concern must have been with some branch of organic chemistry. On the whole
column3: little could be learned from the scientific ensemble
column4: which included a gruesome-looking dissecting table; so that the room was really rather a disappointment. Among the books was a tattered old copy of Borellus in black-letter
column5: and it was weirdly interesting to note that Ward had underlined the same passage whose marking had so perturbed good Mr. Merritt at Curwen's farmhouse more than a century and a half before. That older copy
column6: of course
column7: must have perished along with the rest of Curwen's occult library in the final raid. Three archways opened off the laboratory
column8: and these the doctor proceeded to sample in turn. From his cursory survey he saw that two led merely to small storerooms; but these he canvassed with care
column9: remarking the piles of coffins in various stages of damage and shuddering violently at two or three of the few coffin-plates he could decipher. There was much clothing also stored in these rooms
column10: and several new and tightly nailed boxes which he did not stop to investigate. Most interesting of all
column11: perhaps
column12: were some odd bits which he judged to be fragments of old Joseph Curwen's laboratory appliances. These had suffered damage at the hands of the raiders
column13: but were still partly recognisable as the chemical paraphernalia of the Georgian period.

column1: The third archway led to a very sizeable chamber entirely lined with shelves and having in the centre a table bearing two lamps. These lamps Willett lighted
column2: and in their brilliant glow studied the endless shelving which surrounded him. Some of the upper levels were wholly vacant
column3: but most of the space was filled with small odd-looking leaden jars of two general types; one tall and without handles like a Grecian lekythos or oil-jug
column4: and the other with a single handle and proportioned like a Phaleron jug. All had metal stoppers
column5: and were covered with peculiar-looking symbols moulded in low relief. In a moment the doctor noticed that these jugs were classified with great rigidity; all the lekythoi being on one side of the room with a large wooden sign reading ""Custodes"" above them
column6: and all the Phalerons on the other
column7: correspondingly labelled with a sign reading ""Materia"". Each of the jars or jugs
column8: except some on the upper shelves that turned out to be vacant
column9: bore a cardboard tag with a number apparently referring to a catalogue; and Willett resolved to look for the latter presently. For the moment
column10: however
column11: he was more interested in the nature of the array as a whole; and experimentally opened several of the lekythoi and Phalerons at random with a view to a rough generalisation. The result was invariable. Both types of jar contained a small quantity of a single kind of substance; a fine dusty powder of very light weight and of many shades of dull
column12: neutral colour. To the colours which formed the only point of variation there was no apparent method of disposal; and no distinction between what occurred in the lekythoi and what occurred in the Phalerons. A bluish-grey powder might be by the side of a pinkish-white one
column13: and any one in a Phaleron might have its exact counterpart in a lekythos. The most individual feature about the powders was their non-adhesiveness. Willett would pour one into his hand
column14: and upon returning it to its jug would find that no residue whatever remained on its palm.

column1: The meaning of the two signs puzzled him
column2: and he wondered why this battery of chemicals was separated so radically from those in glass jars on the shelves of the laboratory proper. ""Custodes""
column3: ""Materia""; that was the Latin for ""Guards"" and ""Materials""

To give a clear picture of Owen and his ideas we need to see what was happening in Britain at the time.
Owen was born in the late 18th century but lived most of his life in the early 19th century.
England was at that time undergoing a big change.
The whole structure of society was being transformed.
The Industrial Revolution had begun in the second half of the 18th century
column2: industrial cities developed and inventions took over the production of goods that so far had been mainly hand made and many poor workers from the countryside moved into the cities.

column1: There was a great gap between the rich and the poor.

He was born in Wales in 1771.

column1: In certain places I beheld enormous dark cylindrical towers which climbed far above any of the other structures. These appeared to be of a totally unique nature

column1: Primal myth and modern delusion joined in their assumption that mankind is only one—perhaps the least—of the highly evolved and dominant races of this planet’s long and largely unknown career. Things of inconceivable shape
column3: had reared towers to the sky and delved into every secret of Nature before the first amphibian forbear of man had crawled out of the hot sea three hundred million years ago. Some had come down from the stars; a few were as old as the cosmos itself; others had arisen swiftly from terrene germs as far behind the first germs of our life-cycle as those germs are behind ourselves. Spans of thousands of millions of years

column5: were freely spoken of. Indeed

column1: But most of the tales and impressions concerned a relatively late race

column3: which had lived till only fifty million years before the advent of man. This
column4: they indicated

column3: their achievements
column4: their languages
column5: and their psychologies. With this aeon-embracing knowledge
column6: the Great Race chose from every era and life-form such thoughts
column7: arts

column1: In the latter case the course was easier and more material. With suitable mechanical aid a mind would project itself forward in time
column3: extra-sensory way till it approached the desired period. Then
column4: after preliminary trials

column7: in the body of the organism of the future

column1: Meanwhile the displaced mind
column2: thrown back to the displacer’s age and body
column3: would be carefully guarded. It would be kept from harming the body it occupied
column4: and would be drained of all its knowledge by trained questioners. Often it could be questioned in its own language
column5: when previous quests into the future had brought back records of that language. If the mind came from a body whose language the Great Race could not physically reproduce

column1: When the captive mind’s amazement and resentment had worn off
column2: and when (assuming that it came from a body vastly different from the Great Race’s) it had lost its horror at its unfamiliar temporary form
column3: it was permitted to study its new environment and experience a wonder and wisdom approximating that of its displacer. With suitable precautions
column4: and in exchange for suitable services
column5: it was allowed to rove all over the habitable world in titan airships or on the huge boat-like atomic-engined vehicles which traversed the great roads
column6: and to delve freely into the libraries containing the records of the planet’s past and future. This reconciled many captive minds to their lot; since none were other than keen
column7: and to such minds the unveiling of hidden mysteries of earth—closed chapters of inconceivable pasts and dizzying vortices of future time which include the years ahead of their own natural ages—forms always
column8: despite the abysmal horrors often unveiled
column9: the supreme experience of life.

column1: Now and then certain captives were permitted to meet other captive minds seized from the future—to exchange thoughts with consciousnesses living a hundred or a thousand or a million years before or after their own ages. And all were urged to write copiously in their own languages of themselves and their respective periods; such documents to be filed in the great central archives.
It may be added that there was one sad special type of captive whose privileges were far greater than those of the majority. These were the dying permanent exiles
column2: whose bodies in the future had been seized by keen-minded members of the Great Race who
column3: faced with death
column4: sought to escape mental extinction. Such melancholy exiles were not as common as might be expected
column5: since the longevity of the Great Race lessened its love of life—especially among those superior minds capable of projection. From cases of the permanent projection of elder minds arose many of those lasting changes of personality noticed in later history—including mankind’s.

column1: As for the ordinary cases of exploration—when the displacing mind had learned what it wished in the future
column2: it would build an apparatus like that which had started its flight and reverse the process of projection. Once more it would be in its own body in its own age
column3: while the lately captive mind would return to that body of the future to which it properly belonged. Only when one or the other of the bodies had died during the exchange was this restoration impossible. In such cases
column4: of course
column5: the exploring mind had—like those of the death-escapers—to live out an alien-bodied life in the future; or else the captive mind—like the dying permanent exiles—had to end its days in the form and past age of the Great Race.

column1: This fate was least horrible when the captive mind was also of the Great Race—a not infrequent occurrence
column2: since in all its periods that race was intensely concerned with its own future. The number of dying permanent exiles of the Great Race was very slight—largely because of the tremendous penalties attached to displacements of future Great Race minds by the moribund. Through projection
column3: arrangements were made to inflict these penalties on the offending minds in their new future bodies—and sometimes forced re-exchanges were effected. Complex cases of the displacement of exploring or already captive minds by minds in various regions of the past had been known and carefully rectified. In every age since the discovery of mind-projection
column4: a minute but well-recognised element of the population consisted of Great Race minds from past ages
column5: sojourning for a longer or shorter while.

column1: When a captive mind of alien origin was returned to its own body in the future
column2: it was purged by an intricate mechanical hypnosis of all it had learned in the Great Race’s age—this because of certain troublesome consequences inherent in the general carrying forward of knowledge in large quantities. The few existing instances of clear transmission had caused
column3: and would cause at known future times
column4: great disasters. And it was largely in consequence of two cases of the kind (said the old myths) that mankind had learned what it had concerning the Great Race. Of all things surviving physically and directly from that aeon-distant world
column5: there remained only certain ruins of great stones in far places and under the sea
column6: and parts of the text of the frightful Pnakotic Manuscripts.

column1: Thus the returning mind reached its own age with only the faintest and most fragmentary visions of what it had undergone since its seizure. All memories that could be eradicated were eradicated
column2: so that in most cases only a dream-shadowed blank stretched back to the time of the first exchange. Some minds recalled more than others
column3: and the chance joining of memories had at rare times brought hints of the forbidden past to future ages. There probably never was a time when groups or cults did not secretly cherish certain of these hints. In the Necronomicon the presence of such a cult among human beings was suggested—a cult that sometimes gave aid to minds voyaging down the aeons from the days of the Great Race.

column1: And meanwhile the Great Race itself waxed well-nigh omniscient
column2: and turned to the task of setting up exchanges with the minds of other planets
column3: and of exploring their pasts and futures. It sought likewise to fathom the past years and origin of that black
column4: aeon-dead orb in far space whence its own mental heritage had come—for the mind of the Great Race was older than its bodily form. The beings of a dying elder world
column5: wise with the ultimate secrets
column6: had looked ahead for a new world and species wherein they might have long life; and had sent their minds en masse into that future race best adapted to house them—the cone-shaped things that peopled our earth a billion years ago. Thus the Great Race came to be
column7: while the myriad minds sent backward were left to die in the horror of strange shapes. Later the race would again face death
column8: yet would live through another forward migration of its best minds into the bodies of others who had a longer physical span ahead of them.

column1: Despite the seeming cumbrousness of these explanations

Suppose I did see strange things at night? These were only what I had heard and read of. Suppose I did have odd loathings and perspectives and pseudo-memories? These

column1: All this time my own part in the dreams seemed to be that of a disembodied consciousness with a range of vision wider than the normal; floating freely about
column2: yet confined to the ordinary avenues and speeds of travel. Not until August

column1: And then the morbid temptation to look down at myself became greater and greater
column2: till one night I could not resist it. At first my downward glance revealed nothing whatever. A moment later I perceived that this was because my head lay at the end of a flexible neck of enormous length. Retracting this neck and gazing down very sharply
column3: I saw the scaly
column4: rugose
column5: iridescent bulk of a vast cone ten feet tall and ten feet wide at the base. That was when I waked half of Arkham with my screaming as I plunged madly up from the abyss of sleep.

column1: Only after weeks of hideous repetition did I grow half-reconciled to these visions of myself in monstrous form. In the dreams I now moved bodily among the other unknown entities
column2: reading terrible books from the endless shelves and writing for hours at the great tables with a stylus managed by the green tentacles that hung down from my head. Snatches of what I read and wrote would linger in my memory. There were horrible annals of other worlds and other universes
column3: and of stirrings of formless life outside of all universes. There were records of strange orders of beings which had peopled the world in forgotten pasts
column4: and frightful chronicles of grotesque-bodied intelligences which would people it millions of years after the death of the last human being. And I learned of chapters in human history whose existence no scholar of today has ever suspected. Most of these writings were in the language of the hieroglyphs; which I studied in a queer way with the aid of droning machines
column5: and which was evidently an agglutinative speech with root systems utterly unlike any found in human languages. Other volumes were in other unknown tongues learned in the same queer way. A very few were in languages I knew. Extremely clever pictures
column6: both inserted in the records and forming separate collections
column7: aided me immensely. And all the time I seemed to be setting down a history of my own age in English. On waking
column8: I could recall only minute and meaningless scraps of the unknown tongues which my dream-self had mastered

column1: I learned—even before my waking self had studied the parallel cases or the old myths from which the dreams doubtless sprang—that the entities around me were of the world’s greatest race
column2: which had conquered time and had sent exploring minds into every age. I knew
column3: too

column5: and that a few of the other strange forms housed similarly captured minds. I seemed to talk
column6: in some odd language of claw-clickings
column7: with exiled intellects from every corner of the solar system.

column1: There was a mind from the planet we know as Venus
column2: which would live incalculable epochs to come

column1: The vast

column1: Whence could come the dense personnel of such a column as I now beheld? Did those ancient

column3: uncatalogued
column4: and unsuspected life? Or had some unseen ship indeed landed a legion of unknown outsiders on that hellish reef? Who were they? Why were they here? And if such a column of them was scouring the Ipswich road

column1: I had entered the brush-grown cut and was struggling along at a very slow pace when that damnable fishy odour again waxed dominant. Had the wind suddenly changed eastward

column1: The stench waxed overpowering

So far I had seen none of the lower animals in Innsmouth. That flopping or pattering was monstrous--I could not look upon the degenerate creatures responsible for it. I would keep my eyes shut till the sound receded toward the west. The horde was very close now--air foul with their hoarse snarlings

column1: I am not even yet willing to say whether what followed was a hideous actuality or only a nightmare hallucination. The later action of the government

column4: haunted
column5: and shadowed town? Such places have strange properties

Who can be sure of reality after hearing things like the tale of old Zadok Allen? The government men never found poor Zadok
column8: and have no conjectures to make as to what became of him. Where does madness leave off and reality begin? Is it possible that even my latest fear is sheer delusion?

column2: baying entities of unknown source flopped noisomely past
column3: scarcely more than a hundred yards away?

column1: I thought I was prepared for the worst

Then I knew that a long section of them must be plainly in sight where the sides of the cut flattened out and the road crossed the track--and I could no longer keep myself from sampling whatever horror that leering yellow moon might have to shew.
It was the end

It seemed to me that there were limitless swarms of them and certainly my momentary glimpse could have shewn only the least fraction. In another instant everything was blotted out by a merciful fit of fainting; the first I had ever had."\"﻿West of Arkham the hills rise wild

column1: There was once a road over the hills and through the valleys
column2: that ran straight where the blasted heath is now; but people ceased to use it and a new road was laid curving far toward the south. Traces of the old one can still be found amidst the weeds of a returning wilderness

Then the dark woods will be cut down and the blasted heath will slumber far below blue waters whose surface will mirror the sky and ripple in the sun. And the secrets of the strange days will be one with the deep's secrets; one with the hidden lore of old ocean
column4: and all the mystery of primal earth.

column1: When I went into the hills and vales to survey for the new reservoir they told me the place was evil. They told me this in Arkham

column3: and I wondered how it had come into the folklore of a Puritan people. Then I saw that dark westward tangle of glens and slopes for myself

column6: and their trunks were too big for any healthy New England wood. There was too much silence in the dim alleys between them
column7: and the floor was too soft with the dank moss and mattings of infinite years of decay.

column1: In the open spaces
column2: mostly along the line of the old road
column3: there were little hillside farms; sometimes with all the buildings standing
column4: sometimes with only one or two
column5: and sometimes with only a lone chimney or fast-filling cellar. Weeds and briers reigned

column1: But even all this was not so bad as the blasted heath. I knew it the moment I came upon it at the bottom of a spacious valley; for no other name could fit such a thing
column2: or any other thing fit such a name. It was as if the poet had coined the phrase from having seen this one particular region. It must
column3: I thought as I viewed it

column3: however

column2: I feigned a matter of business; told him of my surveying
column3: and asked vague questions about the district. He was far brighter and more educated than I had been led to think

Relief was all that he showed; relief at the doom of the dark ancient valleys through which he had roamed all his life. They were better under water now--better under water since the strange days. And with this opening his husky voice sank low

column1: It was then that I heard the story

column3: piece out scientific points which he knew only by a fading parrot memory of professors' talk
column4: or bridge over gaps
column5: where his sense of logic and continuity broke down. When he was done I did not wonder that his mind had snapped a trifle
column6: or that the folk of Arkham would not speak much of the blasted heath. I hurried back before sunset to my hotel

column1: It all began

That was the house which had stood where the blasted heath was to come--the trim white Nahum Gardner house amidst its fertile gardens and orchards.

column8: indeed

No sane wholesome colours were anywhere to be seen except in the green grass and leafage; but everywhere were those hectic and prismatic variants of some diseased
column4: underlying primary tone without a place among the known tints of earth. The ""Dutchman's breeches"" became a thing of sinister menace

It was then that they owned that Thaddeus had been right about the trees. Mrs. Gardner was the next to see it from the window as she watched the swollen boughs of a maple against a moonlit sky. The boughs surely moved

column1: Thaddeus went mad in September after a visit to the well. He had gone with a pail and had come back empty-handed
column3: and sometimes lapsing into an inane titter or a whisper about ""the moving colours down there."" Two in one family was pretty bad

column3: then suddenly began to undergo loathsome changes which no one could explain. Their meat was of course useless
column4: and Nahum was at his wit's end. No rural veterinary would approach his place
column5: and the city veterinary from Arkham was openly baffled. The swine began growing grey and brittle and falling to pieces before they died

column7: for they had never been fed from the tainted vegetation. Then something struck the cows. Certain areas or sometimes the whole body would be uncannily shrivelled or compressed
column8: and atrocious collapses or disintegrations were common. In the last stages--and death was always the result--there would be a greying and turning brittle like that which beset the hogs. There could be no question of poison

column12: three in number
column13: had all vanished one night and were never heard of again. The five cats had left some time before

column1: On the nineteenth of October Nahum staggered into Ammi's house with hideous news. The death had come to poor Thaddeus in his attic room

He had come of late to do nothing but stare into space and obey what his father told him; and Ammi thought that his fate was very merciful. Now and then Merwin's screams were answered faintly from the attic

column4: and had never come back. He'd been going to pieces for days

column1: For over two weeks Ammi saw nothing of Nahum; and then

column6: and great bare trees clawing up at the grey November sky with a studied malevolence which Ammi could not but feel had come from some subtle change in the tilt of the branches. But Nahum was alive
column7: after all. He was weak
column8: and lying on a couch in the low-ceiled kitchen
column9: but perfectly conscious and able to give simple orders to Zenas. The room was deadly cold; and as Ammi visibly shivered

column11: indeed

column13: with a cloud of soot blowing about in the chill wind that came down the chimney. Presently Nahum asked him if the extra wood had made him any more comfortable

column4: here she is!"" was the surprised response of poor Nahum

column7: and no sound could be heard from any direction. Of the four doors in sight

column1: It was quite dark inside
column2: for the window was small and half-obscured by the crude wooden bars; and Ammi could see nothing at all on the wide-planked floor. The stench was beyond enduring
column3: and before proceeding further he had to retreat to another room and return with his lungs filled with breathable air. When he did enter he saw something dark in the corner
column4: and upon seeing it more clearly he screamed outright. While he screamed he thought a momentary cloud eclipsed the window
column5: and a second later he felt himself brushed as if by some hateful current of vapour. Strange colours danced before his eyes; and had not a present horror numbed him he would have thought of the globule in the meteor that the geologist's hammer had shattered
column6: and of the morbid vegetation that had sprouted in the spring. As it was he thought only of the blasphemous monstrosity which confronted him
column7: and which all too clearly had shared the nameless fate of young Thaddeus and the livestock. But the terrible thing about the horror was that it very slowly and perceptibly moved as it continued to crumble.

column1: Ammi would give me no added particulars of this scene
column2: but the shape in the comer does not reappear in his tale as a moving object. There are things which cannot be mentioned
column3: and what is done in common humanity is sometimes cruelly judged by the law. I gathered that no moving thing was left in that attic room
column4: and that to leave anything capable of motion there would have been a deed so monstrous as to damn any accountable being to eternal torment. Anyone but a stolid farmer would have fainted or gone mad
column5: but Ammi walked conscious through that low doorway and locked the accursed secret behind him. There would be Nahum to deal with now; he must be fed and tended

column1: Commencing his descent of the dark stairs. Ammi heard a thud below him. He even thought a scream had been suddenly choked off
column2: and recalled nervously the clammy vapour which had brushed by him in that frightful room above. What presence had his cry and entry started up? Halted by some vague fear
column3: he heard still further sounds below. Indubitably there was a sort of heavy dragging
column4: and a most detestably sticky noise as of some fiendish and unclean species of suction. With an associative sense goaded to feverish heights
column5: he thought unaccountably of what he had seen upstairs. Good God! What eldritch dream-world was this into which he had blundered? He dared move neither backward nor forward

column11: exposed laths

column1: But that was all. That which spoke could speak no more because it had completely caved in. Ammi laid a red checked tablecloth over what was left and reeled out the back door into the fields. He climbed the slope to the ten-acre pasture and stumbled home by the north road and the woods. He could not pass that well from which his horses had run away. He had looked at it through the window

column5: and could find no convincing common element to link the strange vegetable conditions

But what peculiar madness could have made both boys jump into the well? Their deeds were so similar-and the fragments showed that they had both suffered from the grey brittle death. Why was everything so grey and brittle?

column1: It was the coroner

column1: Derby’s parents took him abroad every summer

column1: Derby went through Miskatonic University in Arkham
column2: since his parents would not let him board away from them. He entered at sixteen and completed his course in three years

column4: the Unaussprechlichen Kulten of von Junzt

column8: after him.

column1: By the time he was twenty-five Edward Derby was a prodigiously learned man and a fairly well-known poet and fantaisiste

column4: inertia

column1: So the years wore on. Edward’s mother died when he was thirty-four

Some of the whispered rumours about the wild Miskatonic set were extremely singular. There was even talk of black magic and of happenings utterly beyond credibility.

column6: defeat

column8: muddled eyes of poor Edward were gazing out from it.

column2: and his hints occasionally became concrete. What he said was not to be believed
column3: even in centuried and legend-haunted Arkham; but he threw out his dark lore with a sincerity and convincingness which made one fear for his sanity. He talked about terrible meetings in lonely places
column4: of Cyclopean ruins in the heart of the Maine woods beneath which vast staircases lead down to abysses of nighted secrets
column5: of complex angles that lead through invisible walls to other regions of space and time
column6: and of hideous exchanges of personality that permitted explorations in remote and forbidden places
column7: on other worlds

column2: whose insane curves and surfaces answered no conceivable purpose and followed no conceivable geometry. These things
column3: he said
column4: came ‘from outside’; and his wife knew how to get them. Sometimes—but always in frightened and ambiguous whispers—he would suggest things about old Ephraim Waite
column5: whom he had seen occasionally at the college library in the old days. These adumbrations were never specific
column6: but seemed to revolve around some especially horrible doubt as to whether the old wizard were really dead—in a spiritual as well as corporeal sense.

column6: some invisible force would generally clog his motions or make him forget his destination for the time being. His visits usually came when Asenath was away—‘away in her own body’

column1: IV.
Derby had been married more than three years on that August day when I got the telegram from Maine. I had not seen him for two months
column2: but had heard he was away “on business”. Asenath was supposed to be with him
column3: though watchful gossips declared there was someone upstairs in the house behind the doubly curtained windows. They had watched the purchases made by the servants. And now the town marshal of Chesuncook had wired of the draggled madman who stumbled out of the woods with delirious ravings and screamed to me for protection. It was Edward—and he had been just able to recall his own name and my name and address.

column1: “This trip was a bit queer

column3: and all that—which mean a good deal in folklore

column1: I do not recall just what my own part of the conversation was
column2: for the baffling alienage of my seatmate filled all my consciousness. With every moment my feeling of elusive cosmic horror increased

column1: At the junction where the main highway runs inland and avoids Innsmouth I was half afraid my driver would take the bleak shore road that goes through that damnable place. He did not
column3: but darted rapidly past Rowley and Ipswich toward our destination. We reached Arkham before midnight
column4: and found the lights still on at the old Crowninshield house. Derby left the car with a hasty repetition of his thanks

column1: V.
The next two months were full of rumours. People spoke of seeing Derby more and more in his new energised state
column2: and Asenath was scarcely ever in to her few callers. I had only one visit from Edward
column3: when he called briefly in Asenath’s car—duly reclaimed from wherever he had left it in Maine—to get some books he had lent me. He was in his new state
column4: and paused only long enough for some evasively polite remarks. It was plain that he had nothing to discuss with me when in this condition—and I noticed that he did not even trouble to give the old three-and-two signal when ringing the doorbell. As on that evening in the car

column6: infinitely deep horror which I could not explain; so that his swift departure was a prodigious relief.

column1: In mid-September Derby was away for a week
column2: and some of the decadent college set talked knowingly of the matter—hinting at a meeting with a notorious cult-leader
column3: lately expelled from England
column4: who had established headquarters in New York. For my part I could not get that strange ride from Maine out of my head. The transformation I had witnessed had affected me profoundly
column5: and I caught myself again and again trying to account for the thing—and for the extreme horror it had inspired in me.

column1: But the oddest rumours were those about the sobbing in the old Crowninshield house. The voice seemed to be a woman’s

column4: but this was dispelled one day when Asenath appeared in the streets and chatted in a sprightly way with a large number of acquaintances—apologising for her recent absences and speaking incidentally about the nervous breakdown and hysteria of a guest from Boston. The guest was never seen

column1: One evening in mid-October I heard the familiar three-and-two ring at the front door. Answering it myself

column1: Following me clumsily to the study

column3: and I made her promise to stop preying on me. Of course I had certain—certain occult defences I never told you about. She had to give in

column4: and in a flash I was back at the house—in the library where those damned servants had me locked up—and in that cursed fiend’s body . . . that isn’t even human. . . . You know

column2: I had known the difference—yet could I accept an explanation as insane as this? But my distracted caller was growing even wilder.

column1: “I had to save myself—I had to

column3: and the sacrifice would have clinched things. She’d have got me for good . . . she’d have been I
column4: and I’d have been she . . . forever . . . too late. . . . My body’d have been hers for good. . . . She’d have been a man
column5: and fully human

column7: damn her
column8: just as she did before—just as she
column9: he
column10: or it did before. . . .”

column5: just as she almost got mine
column6: and then poisoned the old body he’d put her into. Haven’t you seen old Ephraim’s soul glaring out of that she-devil’s eyes dozens of times . . . and out of mine when she had control of my body?”

column2: and paused for breath. I said nothing

column4: I reflected

column1: “I’ll tell you more later—I must have a long rest now. I’ll tell you something of the forbidden horrors she led me into—something of the age-old horrors that even now are festering in out-of-the-way corners with a few monstrous priests to keep them alive. Some people know things about the universe that nobody ought to know

column7: you know—that might misunderstand our breaking up . . . some of them have damnably curious ideas and methods. I know you’ll stand by me if anything happens—even if I have to tell you a lot that will shock you. . . .”

column2: and in the morning he seemed calmer. We discussed certain possible arrangements for his moving back into the Derby mansion
column3: and I hoped he would lose no time in making the change. He did not call the next evening

column2: for I saw that the subject was a peculiarly disturbing one. Gossip
column3: of course
column4: was rife; but that was no novelty in connexion with the strange ménage at the old Crowninshield house. One thing I did not like was what Derby’s banker let fall in an overexpansive mood at the Miskatonic Club—about the cheques Edward was sending regularly to a Moses and Abigail Sargent and a Eunice Babson in Innsmouth. That looked as if those evil-faced servants were extorting some kind of tribute from him—yet he had not mentioned the matter to me.

column1: I wished that the summer—and my son’s Harvard vacation—would come
column2: so that we could get Edward to Europe. He was not
column3: I soon saw

column5: while his moods of fright and depression were altogether too frequent. The old Derby house was ready by December

column10: looked odd and unwholesome to him. I wondered if Asenath had been writing disturbing letters

column1: VI.

It was about Christmas that Derby broke down one evening while calling on me. I was steering the conversation toward next summer’s travels when he suddenly shrieked and leaped up from his chair with a look of shocking
column2: uncontrollable fright—a cosmic panic and loathing such as only the nether gulfs of nightmare could bring to any sane mind.

column1: “My brain! My brain! God
column2: Dan—it’s tugging—from beyond—knocking—clawing—that she-devil—even now—Ephraim—Kamog! Kamog!—The pit of the shoggoths—Iä! Shub-Niggurath! The Goat with a Thousand Young! . . .

column1: “The flame—the flame . . . beyond body
column2: beyond life . . . in the earth . . . oh

column1: I pulled him back to his chair and poured some wine down his throat as his frenzy sank to a dull apathy. He did not resist
column2: but kept his lips moving as if talking to himself. Presently I realised that he was trying to talk to me
column3: and bent my ear to his mouth to catch the feeble words.

column1: “ . . . again
column2: again . . . she’s trying . . . I might have known . . . nothing can stop that force; not distance
column3: nor magic
column4: nor death . . . it comes and comes
column5: mostly in the night . . . I can’t leave . . . it’s horrible . . . oh
column6: God
column7: Dan
column8: if you only knew as I do just how horrible it is. . . .”

column3: and wished to give nature a chance if I possibly could. He waked at midnight
column4: and I put him to bed upstairs

column6: when called on the wire
column7: said he was at home pacing restlessly about the library.

column2: but I went daily to see him. He would always be sitting in his library
column3: staring at nothing and having an air of abnormal listening. Sometimes he talked rationally
column4: but always on trivial topics. Any mention of his trouble
column5: of future plans
column6: or of Asenath would send him into a frenzy. His butler said he had frightful seizures at night

column1: I had a long talk with his doctor
column3: and lawyer
column4: and finally took the physician with two specialist colleagues to visit him. The spasms that resulted from the first questions were violent and pitiable—and that evening a closed car took his poor struggling body to the Arkham Sanitarium. I was made his guardian and called on him twice weekly—almost weeping to hear his wild shrieks
column5: awesome whispers
column6: and dreadful
column7: droning repetitions of such phrases as “I had to do it—I had to do it . . . it’ll get me . . . it’ll get me . . . down there . . . down there in the dark. . . . Mother
column8: mother! Dan! Save me . . . save me. . . .”

column1: How much hope of recovery there was
column2: no one could say; but I tried my best to be optimistic. Edward must have a home if he emerged
column3: so I transferred his servants to the Derby mansion
column4: which would surely be his sane choice. What to do about the Crowninshield place with its complex arrangements and collections of utterly inexplicable objects I could not decide
column5: so left it momentarily untouched—telling the Derby housemaid to go over and dust the chief rooms once a week
column6: and ordering the furnace man to have a fire on those days.

column1: The final nightmare came before Candlemas—heralded
column3: by a false gleam of hope. One morning late in January the sanitarium telephoned to report that Edward’s reason had suddenly come back. His continuous memory
column4: they said
column5: was badly impaired; but sanity itself was certain. Of course he must remain some time for observation
column6: but there could be little doubt of the outcome. All going well
column7: he would surely be free in a week.

column1: I hastened over in a flood of delight
column2: but stood bewildered when a nurse took me to Edward’s room. The patient rose to greet me
column3: extending his hand with a polite smile; but I saw in an instant that he bore the strangely energised personality which had seemed so foreign to his own nature—the competent personality I had found so vaguely horrible
column4: and which Edward himself had once vowed was the intruding soul of his wife. There was the same blazing vision—so like Asenath’s and old Ephraim’s—and the same firm mouth; and when he spoke I could sense the same grim
column5: pervasive irony in his voice—the deep irony so redolent of potential evil. This was the person who had driven my car through the night five months before—the person I had not seen since that brief call when he had forgotten the old-time doorbell signal and stirred such nebulous fears in me—and now he filled me with the same dim feeling of blasphemous alienage and ineffable cosmic hideousness.

column1: He spoke affably of arrangements for release—and there was nothing for me to do but assent
column2: despite some remarkable gaps in his recent memories. Yet I felt that something was terribly
column3: inexplicably wrong and abnormal. There were horrors in this thing that I could not reach. This was a sane person—but was it indeed the Edward Derby I had known? If not
column4: who or what was it—and where was Edward? Ought it to be free or confined . . . or ought it to be extirpated from the face of the earth? There was a hint of the abysmally sardonic in everything the creature said—the Asenath-like eyes lent a special and baffling mockery to certain words about the ‘early liberty earned by an especially close confinement’. I must have behaved very awkwardly
column5: and was glad to beat a retreat.

column1: All that day and the next I racked my brain over the problem. What had happened? What sort of mind looked out through those alien eyes in Edward’s face? I could think of nothing but this dimly terrible enigma
column2: and gave up all efforts to perform my usual work. The second morning the hospital called up to say that the recovered patient was unchanged
column3: and by evening I was close to a nervous collapse—a state I admit
column4: though others will vow it coloured my subsequent vision. I have nothing to say on this point except that no madness of mine could account for all the evidence.

column1: VII.
It was in the night—after that second evening—that stark
column2: utter horror burst over me and weighted my spirit with a black
column3: clutching panic from which it can never shake free. It began with a telephone call just before midnight. I was the only one up
column4: and sleepily took down the receiver in the library. No one seemed to be on the wire
column5: and I was about to hang up and go to bed when my ear caught a very faint suspicion of sound at the other end. Was someone trying under great difficulties to talk? As I listened I thought I heard a sort of half-liquid bubbling noise—“glub . . . glub . . . glub”—which had an odd suggestion of inarticulate
column6: unintelligible word and syllable divisions. I called
column7: “Who is it?” But the only answer was “glub-glub . . . glub-glub.” I could only assume that the noise was mechanical; but fancying that it might be a case of a broken instrument able to receive but not to send
column8: I added

column5: Asenath

column1: Piecing together the scattered records

I myself had read and heard all the early tales during my memory lapse—my quest had amply proved that. Was it not natural

column1: Primal myth and modern delusion joined in their assumption that mankind is only one—perhaps the least—of the highly evolved and dominant races of this planet’s long and largely unknown career. Things of inconceivable shape
column3: had reared towers to the sky and delved into every secret of Nature before the first amphibian forbear of man had crawled out of the hot sea three hundred million years ago. Some had come down from the stars; a few were as old as the cosmos itself; others had arisen swiftly from terrene germs as far behind the first germs of our life-cycle as those germs are behind ourselves. Spans of thousands of millions of years
column4: and linkages with other galaxies and universes
column5: were freely spoken of. Indeed
column6: there was no such thing as time in its humanly accepted sense.

column1: But most of the tales and impressions concerned a relatively late race
column2: of a queer and intricate shape resembling no life-form known to science
column3: which had lived till only fifty million years before the advent of man. This
column4: they indicated
column5: was the greatest race of all; because it alone had conquered the secret of time. It had learned all things that ever were known or ever would be known on the earth
column6: through the power of its keener minds to project themselves into the past and future
column7: even through gulfs of millions of years
column8: and study the lore of every age. From the accomplishments of this race arose all legends of prophets

column1: In its vast libraries were volumes of texts and pictures holding the whole of earth’s annals—histories and descriptions of every species that had ever been or that ever would be
column2: with full records of their arts
column3: their achievements
column4: their languages
column5: and their psychologies. With this aeon-embracing knowledge
column6: the Great Race chose from every era and life-form such thoughts
column7: arts

column10: was harder to glean than knowledge of the future.

column1: In the latter case the course was easier and more material. With suitable mechanical aid a mind would project itself forward in time
column3: extra-sensory way till it approached the desired period. Then
column4: after preliminary trials
column5: it would seize on the best discoverable representative of the highest of that period’s life-forms; entering the organism’s brain and setting up therein its own vibrations while the displaced mind would strike back to the period of the displacer
column6: remaining in the latter’s body till a reverse process was set up. The projected mind
column7: in the body of the organism of the future
column8: would then pose as a member of the race whose outward form it wore; learning as quickly as possible all that could be learned of the chosen age and its massed information and techniques.

column1: Meanwhile the displaced mind
column2: thrown back to the displacer’s age and body
column3: would be carefully guarded. It would be kept from harming the body it occupied
column4: and would be drained of all its knowledge by trained questioners. Often it could be questioned in its own language
column5: when previous quests into the future had brought back records of that language. If the mind came from a body whose language the Great Race could not physically reproduce
column6: clever machines would be made

column8: and with head and other organs attached to foot-thick
