column10: and walked by the expansion and contraction of a viscous layer attached to their vast ten-foot bases.

column1: When the captive mind’s amazement and resentment had worn off
column2: and when (assuming that it came from a body vastly different from the Great Race’s) it had lost its horror at its unfamiliar temporary form
column3: it was permitted to study its new environment and experience a wonder and wisdom approximating that of its displacer. With suitable precautions
column4: and in exchange for suitable services
column5: it was allowed to rove all over the habitable world in titan airships or on the huge boat-like atomic-engined vehicles which traversed the great roads
column6: and to delve freely into the libraries containing the records of the planet’s past and future. This reconciled many captive minds to their lot; since none were other than keen
column7: and to such minds the unveiling of hidden mysteries of earth—closed chapters of inconceivable pasts and dizzying vortices of future time which include the years ahead of their own natural ages—forms always
column8: despite the abysmal horrors often unveiled
column9: the supreme experience of life.

column1: Now and then certain captives were permitted to meet other captive minds seized from the future—to exchange thoughts with consciousnesses living a hundred or a thousand or a million years before or after their own ages. And all were urged to write copiously in their own languages of themselves and their respective periods; such documents to be filed in the great central archives.
It may be added that there was one sad special type of captive whose privileges were far greater than those of the majority. These were the dying permanent exiles
column2: whose bodies in the future had been seized by keen-minded members of the Great Race who
column3: faced with death
column4: sought to escape mental extinction. Such melancholy exiles were not as common as might be expected
column5: since the longevity of the Great Race lessened its love of life—especially among those superior minds capable of projection. From cases of the permanent projection of elder minds arose many of those lasting changes of personality noticed in later history—including mankind’s.

column1: As for the ordinary cases of exploration—when the displacing mind had learned what it wished in the future
column2: it would build an apparatus like that which had started its flight and reverse the process of projection. Once more it would be in its own body in its own age
column3: while the lately captive mind would return to that body of the future to which it properly belonged. Only when one or the other of the bodies had died during the exchange was this restoration impossible. In such cases
column4: of course
column5: the exploring mind had—like those of the death-escapers—to live out an alien-bodied life in the future; or else the captive mind—like the dying permanent exiles—had to end its days in the form and past age of the Great Race.

column1: This fate was least horrible when the captive mind was also of the Great Race—a not infrequent occurrence
column2: since in all its periods that race was intensely concerned with its own future. The number of dying permanent exiles of the Great Race was very slight—largely because of the tremendous penalties attached to displacements of future Great Race minds by the moribund. Through projection
column3: arrangements were made to inflict these penalties on the offending minds in their new future bodies—and sometimes forced re-exchanges were effected. Complex cases of the displacement of exploring or already captive minds by minds in various regions of the past had been known and carefully rectified. In every age since the discovery of mind-projection
column4: a minute but well-recognised element of the population consisted of Great Race minds from past ages
column5: sojourning for a longer or shorter while.

column1: When a captive mind of alien origin was returned to its own body in the future
column2: it was purged by an intricate mechanical hypnosis of all it had learned in the Great Race’s age—this because of certain troublesome consequences inherent in the general carrying forward of knowledge in large quantities. The few existing instances of clear transmission had caused
column3: and would cause at known future times
column4: great disasters. And it was largely in consequence of two cases of the kind (said the old myths) that mankind had learned what it had concerning the Great Race. Of all things surviving physically and directly from that aeon-distant world
column5: there remained only certain ruins of great stones in far places and under the sea
column6: and parts of the text of the frightful Pnakotic Manuscripts.

column1: Thus the returning mind reached its own age with only the faintest and most fragmentary visions of what it had undergone since its seizure. All memories that could be eradicated were eradicated
column2: so that in most cases only a dream-shadowed blank stretched back to the time of the first exchange. Some minds recalled more than others
column3: and the chance joining of memories had at rare times brought hints of the forbidden past to future ages. There probably never was a time when groups or cults did not secretly cherish certain of these hints. In the Necronomicon the presence of such a cult among human beings was suggested—a cult that sometimes gave aid to minds voyaging down the aeons from the days of the Great Race.

column1: And meanwhile the Great Race itself waxed well-nigh omniscient
column2: and turned to the task of setting up exchanges with the minds of other planets
column3: and of exploring their pasts and futures. It sought likewise to fathom the past years and origin of that black
column4: aeon-dead orb in far space whence its own mental heritage had come—for the mind of the Great Race was older than its bodily form. The beings of a dying elder world
column5: wise with the ultimate secrets
column6: had looked ahead for a new world and species wherein they might have long life; and had sent their minds en masse into that future race best adapted to house them—the cone-shaped things that peopled our earth a billion years ago. Thus the Great Race came to be
column7: while the myriad minds sent backward were left to die in the horror of strange shapes. Later the race would again face death
column8: yet would live through another forward migration of its best minds into the bodies of others who had a longer physical span ahead of them.

column1: Despite the seeming cumbrousness of these explanations

column1: All this time my own part in the dreams seemed to be that of a disembodied consciousness with a range of vision wider than the normal; floating freely about
column2: yet confined to the ordinary avenues and speeds of travel. Not until August
column4: did any suggestions of bodily existence begin to harass me. I say harass
column5: because the first phase was a purely abstract though infinitely terrible association of my previously noted body-loathing with the scenes of my visions. For a while my chief concern during dreams was to avoid looking down at myself

column1: And then the morbid temptation to look down at myself became greater and greater
column2: till one night I could not resist it. At first my downward glance revealed nothing whatever. A moment later I perceived that this was because my head lay at the end of a flexible neck of enormous length. Retracting this neck and gazing down very sharply
column3: I saw the scaly
column4: rugose
column5: iridescent bulk of a vast cone ten feet tall and ten feet wide at the base. That was when I waked half of Arkham with my screaming as I plunged madly up from the abyss of sleep.

column1: Only after weeks of hideous repetition did I grow half-reconciled to these visions of myself in monstrous form. In the dreams I now moved bodily among the other unknown entities
column2: reading terrible books from the endless shelves and writing for hours at the great tables with a stylus managed by the green tentacles that hung down from my head. Snatches of what I read and wrote would linger in my memory. There were horrible annals of other worlds and other universes
column3: and of stirrings of formless life outside of all universes. There were records of strange orders of beings which had peopled the world in forgotten pasts
column4: and frightful chronicles of grotesque-bodied intelligences which would people it millions of years after the death of the last human being. And I learned of chapters in human history whose existence no scholar of today has ever suspected. Most of these writings were in the language of the hieroglyphs; which I studied in a queer way with the aid of droning machines
column5: and which was evidently an agglutinative speech with root systems utterly unlike any found in human languages. Other volumes were in other unknown tongues learned in the same queer way. A very few were in languages I knew. Extremely clever pictures
column6: both inserted in the records and forming separate collections
column7: aided me immensely. And all the time I seemed to be setting down a history of my own age in English. On waking

A recent conversation with Dr. E. M. Boyle of Perth
column2: and some papers with your articles which he has just sent me

column1: The blackfellows have always been full of talk about “great stones with marks on them”
column2: and seem to have a terrible fear of such things. They connect them in some way with their common racial legends about Buddai
column3: the gigantic old man who lies asleep for ages underground with his head on his arm
column4: and who will some day awake and eat up the world. There are some very old and half-forgotten tales of enormous underground huts of great stones
column5: where passages lead down and down
column6: and where horrible things have happened. The blackfellows claim that once some warriors
column7: fleeing in battle
column8: went down into one and never came back
column9: but that frightful winds began to blow from the place soon after they went down. However
column10: there usually isn’t much in what these natives say.

column1: But what I have to tell is more than this. Two years ago
column2: when I was prospecting about 500 miles east in the desert
column3: I came on a lot of queer pieces of dressed stone perhaps 3 × 2 × 2 feet in size
column4: and weathered and pitted to the very limit. At first I couldn’t find any of the marks the blackfellows told about

column1: When I saw some

column4: even in daylight

column6: and sometimes the illusion of such things was agonisingly realistic.

column1: However

column4: sharp-fanged

column1: Gilman dropped in at a doctor’s office on the 16th of the month

column3: and advised him to see a nerve specialist. On reflection

column5: who had curtailed his activities before
column6: would have made him take a rest—an impossible thing now that he was so close to great results in his equations. He was certainly near the boundary between the known universe and the fourth dimension
column7: and who could say how much farther he might go?

column1: But even as these thoughts came to him he wondered at the source of his strange confidence. Did all of this perilous sense of imminence come from the formulae on the sheets he covered day by day? The soft
column3: imaginary footsteps in the sealed loft above were unnerving. And now
column4: too
column5: there was a growing feeling that somebody was constantly persuading him to do something terrible which he could not do. How about the somnambulism? Where did he go sometimes in the night? And what was that faint suggestion of sound which once in a while seemed to trickle through the maddening confusion of identifiable sounds even in broad daylight and full wakefulness? Its rhythm did not correspond to anything on earth
column6: unless perhaps to the cadence of one or two unmentionable Sabbat-chants
column7: and sometimes he feared it corresponded to certain attributes of the vague shrieking or roaring in those wholly alien abysses of dream.

column1: The dreams were meanwhile getting to be atrocious. In the lighter preliminary phase the evil old woman was now of fiendish distinctness

column3: long nose
column4: and shrivelled chin were unmistakable
column5: and her shapeless brown garments were like those he remembered. The expression on her face was one of hideous malevolence and exultation
column6: and when he awaked he could recall a croaking voice that persuaded and threatened. He must meet the Black Man
column7: and go with them all to the throne of Azathoth at the centre of ultimate Chaos. That was what she said. He must sign in his own blood the book of Azathoth and take a new secret name now that his independent delvings had gone so far. What kept him from going with her and Brown Jenkin and the other to the throne of Chaos where the thin flutes pipe mindlessly was the fact that he had seen the name “Azathoth” in the Necronomicon
column8: and knew it stood for a primal evil too horrible for description.

column1: The old woman always appeared out of thin air near the corner where the downward slant met the inward slant. She seemed to crystallise at a point closer to the ceiling than to the floor
column2: and every night she was a little nearer and more distinct before the dream shifted. Brown Jenkin
column3: too
column4: was always a little nearer at the last
column5: and its yellowish-white fangs glistened shockingly in that unearthly violet phosphorescence. Its shrill loathsome tittering stuck more and more in Gilman’s head
column6: and he could remember in the morning how it had pronounced the words “Azathoth” and “Nyarlathotep”.

column1: In the deeper dreams everything was likewise more distinct
column2: and Gilman felt that the twilight abysses around him were those of the fourth dimension. Those organic entities whose motions seemed least flagrantly irrelevant and unmotivated were probably projections of life-forms from our own planet
column3: including human beings. What the others were in their own dimensional sphere or spheres he dared not try to think. Two of the less irrelevantly moving things—a rather large congeries of iridescent
column4: prolately spheroidal bubbles and a very much smaller polyhedron of unknown colours and rapidly shifting surface angles—seemed to take notice of him and follow him about or float ahead as he changed position among the titan prisms
column5: labyrinths
column6: cube-and-plane clusters
column7: and quasi-buildings; and all the while the vague shrieking and roaring waxed louder and louder
column8: as if approaching some monstrous climax of utterly unendurable intensity.

column1: During the night of April 19–20 the new development occurred. Gilman was half-involuntarily moving about in the twilight abysses with the bubble-mass and the small polyhedron floating ahead
column2: when he noticed the peculiarly regular angles formed by the edges of some gigantic neighbouring prism-clusters. In another second he was out of the abyss and standing tremulously on a rocky hillside bathed in intense
column3: diffused green light. He was barefooted and in his night-clothes
column4: and when he tried to walk discovered that he could scarcely lift his feet. A swirling vapour hid everything but the immediate sloping terrain from sight
column5: and he shrank from the thought of the sounds that might surge out of that vapour.

column1: Then he saw the two shapes laboriously crawling toward him—the old woman and the little furry thing. The crone strained up to her knees and managed to cross her arms in a singular fashion
column2: while Brown Jenkin pointed in a certain direction with a horribly anthropoid fore paw which it raised with evident difficulty. Spurred by an impulse he did not originate
column3: Gilman dragged himself forward along a course determined by the angle of the old woman’s arms and the direction of the small monstrosity’s paw
column4: and before he had shuffled three steps he was back in the twilight abysses. Geometrical shapes seethed around him
column5: and he fell dizzily and interminably. At last he woke in his bed in the crazily angled garret of the eldritch old house.

column1: He was good for nothing that morning
column2: and stayed away from all his classes. Some unknown attraction was pulling his eyes in a seemingly irrelevant direction
column3: for he could not help staring at a certain vacant spot on the floor. As the day advanced the focus of his unseeing eyes changed position
column4: and by noon he had conquered the impulse to stare at vacancy. About two o’clock he went out for lunch
column5: and as he threaded the narrow lanes of the city he found himself turning always to the southeast. Only an effort halted him at a cafeteria in Church Street
column6: and after the meal he felt the unknown pull still more strongly.

column1: He would have to consult a nerve specialist after all—perhaps there was a connexion with his somnambulism—but meanwhile he might at least try to break the morbid spell himself. Undoubtedly he could still manage to walk away from the pull; so with great resolution he headed against it and dragged himself deliberately north along Garrison Street. By the time he had reached the bridge over the Miskatonic he was in a cold perspiration
column2: and he clutched at the iron railing as he gazed upstream at the ill-regarded island whose regular lines of ancient standing stones brooded sullenly in the afternoon sunlight.

column1: Then he gave a start. For there was a clearly visible living figure on that desolate island
column2: and a second glance told him it was certainly the strange old woman whose sinister aspect had worked itself so disastrously into his dreams. The tall grass near her was moving
column3: too
column4: as if some other living thing were crawling close to the ground. When the old woman began to turn toward him he fled precipitately off the bridge and into the shelter of the town’s labyrinthine waterfront alleys. Distant though the island was
column5: he felt that a monstrous and invincible evil could flow from the sardonic stare of that bent
column6: ancient figure in brown.

column1: The southeastward pull still held
column2: and only with tremendous resolution could Gilman drag himself into the old house and up the rickety stairs. For hours he sat silent and aimless
column3: with his eyes shifting gradually westward. About six o’clock his sharpened ears caught the whining prayers of Joe Mazurewicz two floors below
column4: and in desperation he seized his hat and walked out into the sunset-golden streets
column5: letting the now directly southward pull carry him where it might. An hour later darkness found him in the open fields beyond Hangman’s Brook
column6: with the glimmering spring stars shining ahead. The urge to walk was gradually changing to an urge to leap mystically into space
column7: and suddenly he realised just where the source of the pull lay.

column1: It was in the sky. A definite point among the stars had a claim on him and was calling him. Apparently it was a point somewhere between Hydra and Argo Navis
column2: and he knew that he had been urged toward it ever since he had awaked soon after dawn. In the morning it had been underfoot; afternoon found it rising in the southeast
column3: and now it was roughly south but wheeling toward the west. What was the meaning of this new thing? Was he going mad? How long would it last? Again mustering his resolution
column4: Gilman turned and dragged himself back to the sinister old house.

column1: Mazurewicz was waiting for him at the door
column2: and seemed both anxious and reluctant to whisper some fresh bit of superstition. It was about the witch light. Joe had been out celebrating the night before—it was Patriots’ Day in Massachusetts—and had come home after midnight. Looking up at the house from outside
column3: he had thought at first that Gilman’s window was dark; but then he had seen the faint violet glow within. He wanted to warn the gentleman about that glow
column4: for everybody in Arkham knew it was Keziah’s witch light which played near Brown Jenkin and the ghost of the old crone herself. He had not mentioned this before
column5: but now he must tell about it because it meant that Keziah and her long-toothed familiar were haunting the young gentleman. Sometimes he and Paul Choynski and Landlord Dombrowski thought they saw that light seeping out of cracks in the sealed loft above the young gentleman’s room
column6: but they had all agreed not to talk about that. However
column7: it would be better for the gentleman to take another room and get a crucifix from some good priest like Father Iwanicki.

column1: As the man rambled on Gilman felt a nameless panic clutch at his throat. He knew that Joe must have been half drunk when he came home the night before
column2: yet this mention of a violet light in the garret window was of frightful import. It was a lambent glow of this sort which always played about the old woman and the small furry thing in those lighter
column3: sharper dreams which prefaced his plunge into unknown abysses
column4: and the thought that a wakeful second person could see the dream-luminance was utterly beyond sane harbourage. Yet where had the fellow got such an odd notion? Had he himself talked as well as walked around the house in his sleep? No
column5: Joe said
column6: he had not—but he must check up on this. Perhaps Frank Elwood could tell him something
column7: though he hated to ask.

column1: Fever—wild dreams—somnambulism—illusions of sounds—a pull toward a point in the sky—and now a suspicion of insane sleep-talking! He must stop studying
column3: and take himself in hand. When he climbed to the second story he paused at Elwood’s door but saw that the other youth was out. Reluctantly he continued up to his garret room and sat down in the dark. His gaze was still pulled to the southwest
column4: but he also found himself listening intently for some sound in the closed loft above
column5: and half imagining that an evil violet light seeped down through an infinitesimal crack in the low
column6: slanting ceiling.

column1: That night as Gilman slept the violet light broke upon him with heightened intensity
column2: and the old witch and small furry thing—getting closer than ever before—mocked him with inhuman squeals and devilish gestures. He was glad to sink into the vaguely roaring twilight abysses
column3: though the pursuit of that iridescent bubble-congeries and that kaleidoscopic little polyhedron was menacing and irritating. Then came the shift as vast converging planes of a slippery-looking substance loomed above and below him—a shift which ended in a flash of delirium and a blaze of unknown
column4: alien light in which yellow
column5: carmine
column6: and indigo were madly and inextricably blended.

column1: He was half lying on a high
column2: fantastically balustraded terrace above a boundless jungle of outlandish
column3: incredible peaks
column4: balanced planes
column5: domes
column6: minarets
column7: horizontal discs poised on pinnacles
column8: and numberless forms of still greater wildness—some of stone and some of metal—which glittered gorgeously in the mixed
column9: almost blistering glare from a polychromatic sky. Looking upward he saw three stupendous discs of flame
column10: each of a different hue
column11: and at a different height above an infinitely distant curving horizon of low mountains. Behind him tiers of higher terraces towered aloft as far as he could see. The city below stretched away to the limits of vision
column12: and he hoped that no sound would well up from it.

column2: polished stone beyond his power to identify
column3: and the tiles were cut in bizarre-angled shapes which struck him as less asymmetrical than based on some unearthly symmetry whose laws he could not comprehend. The balustrade was chest-high
column4: delicate
column5: and fantastically wrought
column6: while along the rail were ranged at short intervals little figures of grotesque design and exquisite workmanship. They
column7: like the whole balustrade
column8: seemed to be made of some sort of shining metal whose colour could not be guessed in this chaos of mixed effulgences; and their nature utterly defied conjecture. They represented some ridged
column9: barrel-shaped object with thin horizontal arms radiating spoke-like from a central ring
column10: and with vertical knobs or bulbs projecting from the head and base of the barrel. Each of these knobs was the hub of a system of five long
column11: flat

column13: but curving slightly away from the central barrel. The base of the bottom knob was fused to the long railing with so delicate a point of contact that several figures had been broken off and were missing. The figures were about four and a half inches in height
column14: while the spiky arms gave them a maximum diameter of about two and a half inches.

column1: When Gilman stood up the tiles felt hot to his bare feet. He was wholly alone
column2: and his first act was to walk to the balustrade and look dizzily down at the endless
column3: Cyclopean city almost two thousand feet below. As he listened he thought a rhythmic confusion of faint musical pipings covering a wide tonal range welled up from the narrow streets beneath
column4: and he wished he might discern the denizens of the place. The sight turned him giddy after a while
column5: so that he would have fallen to the pavement had he not clutched instinctively at the lustrous balustrade. His right hand fell on one of the projecting figures
column6: the touch seeming to steady him slightly. It was too much
column7: however
column8: for the exotic delicacy of the metal-work
column9: and the spiky figure snapped off under his grasp. Still half-dazed
column10: he continued to clutch it as his other hand seized a vacant space on the smooth railing.

column1: But now his oversensitive ears caught something behind him
column2: and he looked back across the level terrace. Approaching him softly though without apparent furtiveness were five figures
column3: two of which were the sinister old woman and the fanged
column4: furry little animal. The other three were what sent him unconscious—for they were living entities about eight feet high
column5: shaped precisely like the spiky images on the balustrade
column6: and propelling themselves by a spider-like wriggling of their lower set of starfish-arms.

column1: Gilman awakened in his bed
column2: drenched by a cold perspiration and with a smarting sensation in his face
column3: hands
column4: and feet. Springing to the floor
column5: he washed and dressed in frantic haste
column6: as if it were necessary for him to get out of the house as quickly as possible. He did not know where he wished to go
column7: but felt that once more he would have to sacrifice his classes. The odd pull toward that spot in the sky between Hydra and Argo had abated
column8: but another of even greater strength had taken its place. Now he felt that he must go north—infinitely north. He dreaded to cross the bridge that gave a view of the desolate island in the Miskatonic
column9: so went over the Peabody Avenue bridge. Very often he stumbled
column10: for his eyes and ears were chained to an extremely lofty point in the blank blue sky.

column1: After about an hour he got himself under better control
column2: and saw that he was far from the city. All around him stretched the bleak emptiness of salt marshes
column3: while the narrow road ahead led to Innsmouth—that ancient
column4: half-deserted town which Arkham people were so curiously unwilling to visit. Though the northward pull had not diminished
column5: he resisted it as he had resisted the other pull
column6: and finally found that he could almost balance the one against the other. Plodding back to town and getting some coffee at a soda fountain
column7: he dragged himself into the public library and browsed aimlessly among the lighter magazines. Once he met some friends who remarked how oddly sunburned he looked
column8: but he did not tell them of his walk. At three o’clock he took some lunch at a restaurant
column9: noting meanwhile that the pull had either lessened or divided itself. After that he killed the time at a cheap cinema show
column10: seeing the inane performance over and over again without paying any attention to it.

column1: About nine at night he drifted homeward and stumbled into the ancient house. Joe Mazurewicz was whining unintelligible prayers
column2: and Gilman hastened up to his own garret chamber without pausing to see if Elwood was in. It was when he turned on the feeble electric light that the shock came. At once he saw there was something on the table which did not belong there
column3: and a second look left no room for doubt. Lying on its side—for it could not stand up alone—was the exotic spiky figure which in his monstrous dream he had broken off the fantastic balustrade. No detail was missing. The ridged
column4: barrel-shaped centre
column5: the thin
column6: radiating arms
column7: the knobs at each end
column8: and the flat
column9: slightly outward-curving starfish-arms spreading from those knobs—all were there. In the electric light the colour seemed to be a kind of iridescent grey veined with green
column10: and Gilman could see amidst his horror and bewilderment that one of the knobs ended in a jagged break corresponding to its former point of attachment to the dream-railing.

column1: Only his tendency toward a dazed stupor prevented him from screaming aloud. This fusion of dream and reality was too much to bear. Still dazed
column2: he clutched at the spiky thing and staggered downstairs to Landlord Dombrowski’s quarters. The whining prayers of the superstitious loomfixer were still sounding through the mouldy halls
column3: but Gilman did not mind them now. The landlord was in
column4: and greeted him pleasantly. No
column5: he had not seen that thing before and did not know anything about it. But his wife had said she found a funny tin thing in one of the beds when she fixed the rooms at noon
column6: and maybe that was it. Dombrowski called her
column7: and she waddled in. Yes
column8: that was the thing. She had found it in the young gentleman’s bed—on the side next the wall. It had looked very queer to her
column9: but of course the young gentleman had lots of queer things in his room—books and curios and pictures and markings on paper. She certainly knew nothing about it.

column1: So Gilman climbed upstairs again in a mental turmoil
column2: convinced that he was either still dreaming or that his somnambulism had run to incredible extremes and led him to depredations in unknown places. Where had he got this outré thing? He did not recall seeing it in any museum in Arkham. It must have been somewhere
column3: though; and the sight of it as he snatched it in his sleep must have caused the odd dream-picture of the balustraded terrace. Next day he would make some very guarded inquiries—and perhaps see the nerve specialist.

column1: Meanwhile he would try to keep track of his somnambulism. As he went upstairs and across the garret hall he sprinkled about some flour which he had borrowed—with a frank admission as to its purpose—from the landlord. He had stopped at Elwood’s door on the way
column2: but had found all dark within. Entering his room
column3: he placed the spiky thing on the table
column4: and lay down in complete mental and physical exhaustion without pausing to undress. From the closed loft above the slanting ceiling he thought he heard a faint scratching and padding
column5: but he was too disorganised even to mind it. That cryptical pull from the north was getting very strong again
column6: though it seemed now to come from a lower place in the sky.

column1: In the dazzling violet light of dream the old woman and the fanged
column2: furry thing came again and with a greater distinctness than on any former occasion. This time they actually reached him
column3: and he felt the crone’s withered claws clutching at him. He was pulled out of bed and into empty space
column4: and for a moment he heard a rhythmic roaring and saw the twilight amorphousness of the vague abysses seething around him. But that moment was very brief
column5: for presently he was in a crude
column6: windowless little space with rough beams and planks rising to a peak just above his head
column7: and with a curious slanting floor underfoot. Propped level on that floor were low cases full of books of every degree of antiquity and disintegration
column8: and in the centre were a table and bench
column9: both apparently fastened in place. Small objects of unknown shape and nature were ranged on the tops of the cases
column10: and in the flaming violet light Gilman thought he saw a counterpart of the spiky image which had puzzled him so horribly. On the left the floor fell abruptly away
column11: leaving a black triangular gulf out of which
column12: after a second’s dry rattling
column13: there presently climbed the hateful little furry thing with the yellow fangs and bearded human face.

column1: The evilly grinning beldame still clutched him
column2: and beyond the table stood a figure he had never seen before—a tall
column3: lean man of dead black colouration but without the slightest sign of negroid features; wholly devoid of either hair or beard
column4: and wearing as his only garment a shapeless robe of some heavy black fabric. His feet were indistinguishable because of the table and bench
column5: but he must have been shod
column6: since there was a clicking whenever he changed position. The man did not speak
column7: and bore no trace of expression on his small
column8: regular features. He merely pointed to a book of prodigious size which lay open on the table
column9: while the beldame thrust a huge grey quill into Gilman’s right hand. Over everything was a pall of intensely maddening fear
column10: and the climax was reached when the furry thing ran up the dreamer’s clothing to his shoulders and then down his left arm
column11: finally biting him sharply in the wrist just below his cuff. As the blood spurted from this wound Gilman lapsed into a faint.

column1: He awaked on the morning of the 22nd with a pain in his left wrist
column2: and saw that his cuff was brown with dried blood. His recollections were very confused
column3: but the scene with the black man in the unknown space stood out vividly. The rats must have bitten him as he slept
column4: giving rise to the climax of that frightful dream. Opening the door
column5: he saw that the flour on the corridor floor was undisturbed except for the huge prints of the loutish fellow who roomed at the other end of the garret. Again he tried to stop up the hole at the base of the slanting wall
column6: wedging in a candlestick which seemed of about the right size. His ears were ringing horribly
column7: as if with the residual echoes of some horrible noise heard in dreams.

column3: which had begun to attack his imagination so violently

column5: twilight abysses
column6: and of still vaster
column7: blacker abysses beyond them—abysses in which all fixed suggestions of form were absent. He had been taken there by the bubble-congeries and the little polyhedron which always dogged him; but they
column8: like himself
column9: had changed to wisps of milky
column10: barely luminous mist in this farther void of ultimate blackness. Something else had gone on ahead—a larger wisp which now and then condensed into nameless approximations of form—and he thought that their progress had not been in a straight line
column11: but rather along the alien curves and spirals of some ethereal vortex which obeyed laws unknown to the physics and mathematics of any conceivable cosmos. Eventually there had been a hint of vast
column12: leaping shadows
column13: of a monstrous
column14: half-acoustic pulsing
column15: and of the thin
column16: monotonous piping of an unseen flute—but that was all. Gilman decided he had picked up that last conception from what he had read in the Necronomicon about the mindless entity Azathoth
column17: which rules all time and space from a curiously environed black throne at the centre of Chaos.

column8: insistent impulse to fly away from his present situation

column1: On the morning of April 27 a fresh rat-hole appeared in the room where Gilman was a guest

Tradition emphasises the uselessness of material barriers in halting a witch’s motions; and who can say what underlies the old tales of broomstick rides through the night?

column5: yanking him out of bed and into empty space. Again the infinitude of the shrieking twilight abysses flashed past him

column7: muddy
column8: unknown alley of foetid odours
column9: with the rotting walls of ancient houses towering up on every hand.

column7: motioning to Gilman to wait and disappearing inside the black aperture.

column1: The youth’s oversensitive ears caught a hideous strangled cry

column3: senseless form which she thrust at the dreamer as if ordering him to carry it. The sight of this form
column4: and the expression on its face
column5: broke the spell. Still too dazed to cry out

column7: shrill tittering of the fanged
column8: rat-like abnormality.

column1: On the morning of the 29th Gilman awaked into a maelstrom of horror. The instant he opened his eyes he knew something was terribly wrong

column5: but he knew at least that he must have been sleep-walking. Elwood had been lost too deeply in slumber to hear and stop him. On the floor were confused muddy prints
column6: but oddly enough they did not extend all the way to the door. The more Gilman looked at them
column7: the more peculiar they seemed; for in addition to those he could recognise as his there were some smaller
column8: almost round markings—such as the legs of a large chair or table might make
column9: except that most of them tended to be divided into halves. There were also some curious muddy rat-tracks leading out of a fresh hole and back into it again. Utter bewilderment and the fear of madness racked Gilman as he staggered to the door and saw that there were no muddy prints outside. The more he remembered of his hideous dream the more terrified he felt
column10: and it added to his desperation to hear Joe Mazurewicz chanting mournfully two floors below.

column1: Descending to Elwood’s room he roused his still-sleeping host and began telling of how he had found himself

column4: and how the muddy

column7: livid marks on his throat
column8: as if he had tried to strangle himself. He put his hands up to them
column9: but found that they did not even approximately fit. While they were talking Desrochers dropped in to say that he had heard a terrific clattering overhead in the dark small hours. No
column10: there had been no one on the stairs after midnight—though just before midnight he had heard faint footfalls in the garret
column11: and cautiously descending steps he did not like. It was
column12: he added
column13: a very bad time of year for Arkham. The young gentleman had better be sure to wear the crucifix Joe Mazurewicz had given him. Even the daytime was not safe
column14: for after dawn there had been strange sounds in the house—especially a thin
column15: childish wail hastily choked off.

column1: Gilman mechanically attended classes that morning
column2: but was wholly unable to fix his mind on his studies. A mood of hideous apprehension and expectancy had seized him
column3: and he seemed to be awaiting the fall of some annihilating blow. At noon he lunched at the University Spa
column4: picking up a paper from the next seat as he waited for dessert. But he never ate that dessert; for an item on the paper’s first page left him limp
column5: wild-eyed
column6: and able only to pay his check and stagger back to Elwood’s room.

column1: There had been a strange kidnapping the night before in Orne’s Gangway
column2: and the two-year-old child of a clod-like laundry worker named Anastasia Wolejko had completely vanished from sight. The mother
column3: it appeared
column4: had feared the event for some time; but the reasons she assigned for her fear were so grotesque that no one took them seriously. She had
column5: she said
column6: seen Brown Jenkin about the place now and then ever since early in March
column7: and knew from its grimaces and titterings that little Ladislas must be marked for sacrifice at the awful Sabbat on Walpurgis-Night. She had asked her neighbour Mary Czanek to sleep in the room and try to protect the child
column8: but Mary had not dared. She could not tell the police
column9: for they never believed such things. Children had been taken that way every year ever since she could remember. And her friend Pete Stowacki would not help because he wanted the child out of the way anyhow.

column1: But what threw Gilman into a cold perspiration was the report of a pair of revellers who had been walking past the mouth of the gangway just after midnight. They admitted they had been drunk
column2: but both vowed they had seen a crazily dressed trio furtively entering the dark passageway. There had
column3: they said
column4: been a huge robed negro
column5: a little old woman in rags
column6: and a young white man in his night-clothes. The old woman had been dragging the youth
column7: while around the feet of the negro a tame rat was rubbing and weaving in the brown mud.

column1: Gilman sat in a daze all the afternoon
column2: and Elwood—who had meanwhile seen the papers and formed terrible conjectures from them—found him thus when he came home. This time neither could doubt but that something hideously serious was closing in around them. Between the phantasms of nightmare and the realities of the objective world a monstrous and unthinkable relationship was crystallising
column3: and only stupendous vigilance could avert still more direful developments. Gilman must see a specialist sooner or later
column4: but not just now
column5: when all the papers were full of this kidnapping business.

column1: Just what had really happened was maddeningly obscure
column2: and for a moment both Gilman and Elwood exchanged whispered theories of the wildest kind. Had Gilman unconsciously succeeded better than he knew in his studies of space and its dimensions? Had he actually slipped outside our sphere to points unguessed and unimaginable? Where—if anywhere—had he been on those nights of daemoniac alienage? The roaring twilight abysses—the green hillside—the blistering terrace—the pulls from the stars—the ultimate black vortex—the black man—the muddy alley and the stairs—the old witch and the fanged
column3: furry horror—the bubble-congeries and the little polyhedron—the strange sunburn—the wrist wound—the unexplained image—the muddy feet—the throat-marks—the tales and fears of the superstitious foreigners—what did all this mean? To what extent could the laws of sanity apply to such a case?

column1: There was no sleep for either of them that night
column2: but next day they both cut classes and drowsed. This was April 30th
column3: and with the dusk would come the hellish Sabbat-time which all the foreigners and the superstitious old folk feared. Mazurewicz came home at six o’clock and said people at the mill were whispering that the Walpurgis-revels would be held in the dark ravine beyond Meadow Hill where the old white stone stands in a place queerly void of all plant-life. Some of them had even told the police and advised them to look there for the missing Wolejko child
column4: but they did not believe anything would be done. Joe insisted that the poor young gentleman wear his nickel-chained crucifix
column5: and Gilman put it on and dropped it inside his shirt to humour the fellow.

column1: Late at night the two youths sat drowsing in their chairs
column2: lulled by the rhythmical praying of the loomfixer on the floor below. Gilman listened as he nodded
column3: his preternaturally sharpened hearing seeming to strain for some subtle
column4: dreaded murmur beyond the noises in the ancient house. Unwholesome recollections of things in the Necronomicon and the Black Book welled up
column5: and he found himself swaying to infandous rhythms said to pertain to the blackest ceremonies of the Sabbat and to have an origin outside the time and space we comprehend.

column1: Presently he realised what he was listening for—the hellish chant of the celebrants in the distant black valley. How did he know so much about what they expected? How did he know the time when Nahab and her acolyte were due to bear the brimming bowl which would follow the black cock and the black goat? He saw that Elwood had dropped asleep
column2: and tried to call out and waken him. Something
column3: however
column4: closed his throat. He was not his own master. Had he signed the black man’s book after all?

column1: Then his fevered

column5: and the dancers must be starting in. How could he keep himself from going? What was it that had enmeshed him? Mathematics—folklore—the house—old Keziah—Brown Jenkin . . . and now he saw that there was a fresh rat-hole in the wall near his couch. Above the distant chanting and the nearer praying of Joe Mazurewicz came another sound—a stealthy
column6: determined scratching in the partitions. He hoped the electric lights would not go out. Then he saw the fanged
column7: bearded little face in the rat-hole—the accursed little face which he at last realised bore such a shocking

column1: The screaming twilight abysses flashed before him
column2: and he felt himself helpless in the formless grasp of the iridescent bubble-congeries. Ahead raced the small
column3: kaleidoscopic polyhedron

column5: ultimate space-time seethings which lie behind the massed spheres of matter and sometimes break forth in measured reverberations that penetrate faintly to every layer of entity and give hideous significance throughout the worlds to certain dreaded periods.

column3: the low cases of ancient books
column4: the bench and table
column5: the queer objects
column6: and the triangular gulf at one side. On the table lay a small white figure—an infant boy
column7: unclothed and unconscious—while on the other side stood the monstrous
column8: leering old woman with a gleaming
column9: grotesque-hafted knife in her right hand
column10: and a queerly proportioned pale metal bowl covered with curiously chased designs and having delicate lateral handles in her left. She was intoning some croaking ritual in a language which Gilman could not understand

column4: grotesque knife above the small white victim as high as her right hand could reach. The fanged
column5: furry thing began tittering a continuation of the unknown ritual
column6: while the witch croaked loathsome responses. Gilman felt a gnawing
column7: poignant abhorrence shoot through his mental and emotional paralysis
column8: and the light metal bowl shook in his grasp. A second later the downward motion of the knife broke the spell completely

column1: In an instant he had edged up the slanting floor around the end of the table and wrenched the knife from the old woman’s claws; sending it clattering over the brink of the narrow triangular gulf. In another instant
column3: matters were reversed; for those murderous claws had locked themselves tightly around his own throat
column4: while the wrinkled face was twisted with insane fury. He felt the chain of the cheap crucifix grinding into his neck
column5: and in his peril wondered how the sight of the object itself would affect the evil creature. Her strength was altogether superhuman
column6: but as she continued her choking he reached feebly in his shirt and drew out the metal symbol
column7: snapping the chain and pulling it free.

column2: and her grip relaxed long enough to give Gilman a chance to break it entirely. He pulled the steel-like claws from his neck
column3: and would have dragged the beldame over the edge of the gulf had not the claws received a fresh access of strength and closed in again. This time he resolved to reply in kind
column4: and his own hands reached out for the creature’s throat. Before she saw what he was doing he had the chain of the crucifix twisted about her neck
column5: and a moment later he had tightened it enough to cut off her breath. During her last struggle he felt something bite at his ankle
column6: and saw that Brown Jenkin had come to her aid. With one savage kick he sent the morbidity over the edge of the gulf and heard it whimper on some level far below.

column1: Whether he had killed the ancient crone he did not know
column2: but he let her rest on the floor where she had fallen. Then
column3: as he turned away
column4: he saw on the table a sight which nearly snapped the last thread of his reason. Brown Jenkin
column5: tough of sinew and with four tiny hands of daemoniac dexterity
column6: had been busy while the witch was throttling him
column7: and his efforts had been in vain. What he had prevented the knife from doing to the victim’s chest
column8: the yellow fangs of the furry blasphemy had done to a wrist—and the bowl so lately on the floor stood full beside the small lifeless body.

column1: In his dream-delirium Gilman heard the hellish
column2: alien-rhythmed chant of the Sabbat coming from an infinite distance
column3: and knew the black man must be there. Confused memories mixed themselves with his mathematics
column4: and he believed his subconscious mind held the angles which he needed to guide him back to the normal world—alone and unaided for the first time. He felt sure he was in the immemorially sealed loft above his own room
column5: but whether he could ever escape through the slanting floor or the long-stopped egress he doubted greatly. Besides
column6: would not an escape from a dream-loft bring him merely into a dream-house—an abnormal projection of the actual place he sought? He was wholly bewildered as to the relation betwixt dream and reality in all his experiences.

column1: The passage through the vague abysses would be frightful
column2: for the Walpurgis-rhythm would be vibrating
column3: and at last he would have to hear that hitherto veiled cosmic pulsing which he so mortally dreaded. Even now he could detect a low
column4: monstrous shaking whose tempo he suspected all too well. At Sabbat-time it always mounted and reached through to the worlds to summon the initiate to nameless rites. Half the chants of the Sabbat were patterned on this faintly overheard pulsing which no earthly ear could endure in its unveiled spatial fulness. Gilman wondered
column5: too
column6: whether he could trust his instinct to take him back to the right part of space. How could he be sure he would not land on that green-litten hillside of a far planet
column7: on the tessellated terrace above the city of tentacled monsters somewhere beyond the galaxy
column8: or in the spiral black vortices of that ultimate void of Chaos wherein reigns the mindless daemon-sultan Azathoth?

column1: Just before he made the plunge the violet light went out and left him in utter blackness. The witch—old Keziah—Nahab—that must have meant her death. And mixed with the distant chant of the Sabbat and the whimpers of Brown Jenkin in the gulf below he thought he heard another and wilder whine from unknown depths. Joe Mazurewicz—the prayers against the Crawling Chaos now turning to an inexplicably triumphant shriek—worlds of sardonic actuality impinging on vortices of febrile dream—Iä! Shub-Niggurath! The Goat with a Thousand Young. . . .
They found Gilman on the floor of his queerly angled old garret room long before dawn

column3: and had even wakened the soundly sleeping Elwood in his chair. He was alive

column5: staring eyes

column8: and Joe’s crucifix was missing. Elwood trembled
column9: afraid even to speculate on what new form his friend’s sleep-walking had taken. Mazurewicz seemed half-dazed because of a “sign” he said he had had in response to his prayers

column1: When the dreamer was settled on his couch in Elwood’s room they sent for Dr. Malkowski—a local practitioner who would repeat no tales where they might prove embarrassing—and he gave Gilman two hypodermic injections which caused him to relax in something like natural drowsiness. During the day the patient regained consciousness at times and whispered his newest dream disjointedly to Elwood. It was a painful process
column2: and at its very start brought out a fresh and disconcerting fact.

column1: Gilman—whose ears had so lately possessed an abnormal sensitiveness—was now stone deaf. Dr. Malkowski
column3: told Elwood that both ear-drums were ruptured
column4: as if by the impact of some stupendous sound intense beyond all human conception or endurance. How such a sound could have been heard in the last few hours without arousing all the Miskatonic Valley was more than the honest physician could say.

column2: so that a fairly easy communication was maintained. Neither knew what to make of the whole chaotic business
column3: and decided it would be better if they thought as little as possible about it. Both
column4: though
column5: agreed that they must leave this ancient and accursed house as soon as it could be arranged. Evening papers spoke of a police raid on some curious revellers in a ravine beyond Meadow Hill just before dawn
column6: and mentioned that the white stone there was an object of age-long superstitious regard. Nobody had been caught

column7: and rushed over to his guest’s couch. The occupant was emitting sounds of veritably inhuman nature
column8: as if racked by some torment beyond description. He was writhing under the bedclothes
column9: and a great red stain was beginning to appear on the blankets.

column2: but gradually the screaming and writhing subsided. By this time Dombrowski
column3: Choynski
column4: Desrochers
column5: Mazurewicz
column6: and the top-floor lodger were all crowding into the doorway
column7: and the landlord had sent his wife back to telephone for Dr. Malkowski. Everybody shrieked when a large rat-like form suddenly jumped out from beneath the ensanguined bedclothes and scuttled across the floor to a fresh

column1: It would be barbarous to do more than suggest what had killed Gilman. There had been virtually a tunnel through his body—something had eaten his heart out. Dombrowski
column2: frantic at the failure of his constant rat-poisoning efforts
column3: cast aside all thought of his lease and within a week had moved with all his older lodgers to a dingy but less ancient house in Walnut Street. The worst thing for a while was keeping Joe Mazurewicz quiet; for the brooding loomfixer would never stay sober
column4: and was constantly whining and muttering about spectral and terrible things.

column1: It seems that on that last hideous night Joe had stooped to look at the crimson rat-tracks which led from Gilman’s couch to the nearby hole. On the carpet they were very indistinct
column2: but a piece of open flooring intervened between the carpet’s edge and the base-board. There Mazurewicz had found something monstrous—or thought he had
column3: for no one else could quite agree with him despite the undeniable queerness of the prints. The tracks on the flooring were certainly vastly unlike the average prints of a rat
column4: but even Choynski and Desrochers would not admit that they were like the prints of four tiny human hands.

column1: The house was never rented again. As soon as Dombrowski left it the pall of its final desolation began to descend
column2: for people shunned it both on account of its old reputation and because of the new foetid odour. Perhaps the ex-landlord’s rat-poison had worked after all
column3: for not long after his departure the place became a neighbourhood nuisance. Health officials traced the smell to the closed spaces above and beside the eastern garret room
column4: and agreed that the number of dead rats must be enormous. They decided
column5: however
column6: that it was not worth their while to hew open and disinfect the long-sealed spaces; for the foetor would soon be over
column7: and the locality was not one which encouraged fastidious standards. Indeed
column8: there were always vague local tales of unexplained stenches upstairs in the Witch House just after May-Eve and Hallowmass. The neighbours grumblingly acquiesced in the inertia—but the foetor none the less formed an additional count against the place. Toward the last the house was condemned as an habitation by the building inspector.

column1: Gilman’s dreams and their attendant circumstances have never been explained. Elwood
column2: whose thoughts on the entire episode are sometimes almost maddening
column3: came back to college the next autumn and graduated in the following June. He found the spectral gossip of the town much diminished

column1: The first half of the principal manuscript told a very peculiar tale. It appears that on March 1st

column9: “It is new

column12: or the contemplative Sphinx

column1: It was then that he began that rambling tale which suddenly played upon a sleeping memory and won the fevered interest of my uncle. There had been a slight earthquake tremor the night before

column5: and from some undetermined point below had come a voice that was not a voice; a chaotic sensation which only fancy could transmute into sound

column3: when waking had stolen bewilderingly over him. My uncle blamed his old age
column4: Wilcox afterward said
column5: for his slowness in recognising both hieroglyphics and pictorial design. Many of his questions seemed highly out-of-place to his visitor

When Professor Angell became convinced that the sculptor was indeed ignorant of any cult or system of cryptic lore

column14: the doctor added

column5: it seems

column1: It was from the artists and poets that the pertinent answers came

column17: however

column1: The press cuttings
column3: touched on cases of panic
column4: mania
column5: and eccentricity during the given period. Professor Angell must have employed a cutting bureau
column6: for the number of extracts was tremendous and the sources scattered throughout the globe. Here was a nocturnal suicide in London
column7: where a lone sleeper had leaped from a window after a shocking cry. Here likewise a rambling letter to the editor of a paper in South America
column8: where a fanatic deduces a dire future from visions he has seen. A despatch from California describes a theosophist colony as donning white robes en masse for some “glorious fulfilment” which never arrives
column9: whilst items from India speak guardedly of serious native unrest toward the end of March. Voodoo orgies multiply in Hayti
column10: and African outposts report ominous mutterings. American officers in the Philippines find certain tribes bothersome about this time

column15: that only a miracle can have stopped the medical fraternity from noting strange parallelisms and drawing mystified conclusions. A weird bunch of cuttings
column16: all told; and I can at this date scarcely envisage the callous rationalism with which I set them aside. But I was then convinced that young Wilcox had known of the older matters mentioned by the professor.

column1: II.
The Tale of Inspector Legrasse.
The older matters which had made the sculptor’s dream and bas-relief so significant to my uncle formed the subject of the second half of his long manuscript. Once before
column3: Professor Angell had seen the hellish outlines of the nameless monstrosity
column4: puzzled over the unknown hieroglyphics
column5: and heard the ominous syllables which can be rendered only as “Cthulhu”; and all this in so stirring and horrible a connexion that it is small wonder he pursued young Wilcox with queries and demands for data.

column1: The earlier experience had come in 1908
column3: when the American Archaeological Society held its annual meeting in St. Louis. Professor Angell
column4: as befitted one of his authority and attainments
column5: had had a prominent part in all the deliberations; and was one of the first to be approached by the several outsiders who took advantage of the convocation to offer questions for correct answering and problems for expert solution.

column1: The chief of these outsiders
column2: and in a short time the focus of interest for the entire meeting
column3: was a commonplace-looking middle-aged man who had travelled all the way from New Orleans for certain special information unobtainable from any local source. His name was John Raymond Legrasse
column4: and he was by profession an Inspector of Police. With him he bore the subject of his visit
column5: a grotesque
column6: repulsive
column7: and apparently very ancient stone statuette whose origin he was at a loss to determine. It must not be fancied that Inspector Legrasse had the least interest in archaeology. On the contrary
column8: his wish for enlightenment was prompted by purely professional considerations. The statuette
column9: idol
column10: fetish
column11: or whatever it was
column12: had been captured some months before in the wooded swamps south of New Orleans during a raid on a supposed voodoo meeting; and so singular and hideous were the rites connected with it
column13: that the police could not but realise that they had stumbled on a dark cult totally unknown to them
column14: and infinitely more diabolic than even the blackest of the African voodoo circles. Of its origin
column15: apart from the erratic and unbelievable tales extorted from the captured members
column16: absolutely nothing was to be discovered; hence the anxiety of the police for any antiquarian lore which might help them to place the frightful symbol
column17: and through it track down the cult to its fountain-head.

column1: Inspector Legrasse was scarcely prepared for the sensation which his offering created. One sight of the thing had been enough to throw the assembled men of science into a state of tense excitement
column2: and they lost no time in crowding around him to gaze at the diminutive figure whose utter strangeness and air of genuinely abysmal antiquity hinted so potently at unopened and archaic vistas. No recognised school of sculpture had animated this terrible object
column3: yet centuries and even thousands of years seemed recorded in its dim and greenish surface of unplaceable stone.

column1: The figure
column2: which was finally passed slowly from man to man for close and careful study
column3: was between seven and eight inches in height
column4: and of exquisitely artistic workmanship. It represented a monster of vaguely anthropoid outline
column5: but with an octopus-like head whose face was a mass of feelers
column6: a scaly
column7: rubbery-looking body
column8: prodigious claws on hind and fore feet
column9: and long
column10: narrow wings behind. This thing
column11: which seemed instinct with a fearsome and unnatural malignancy
column12: was of a somewhat bloated corpulence
column13: and squatted evilly on a rectangular block or pedestal covered with undecipherable characters. The tips of the wings touched the back edge of the block
column14: the seat occupied the centre
column15: whilst the long
column16: curved claws of the doubled-up
column17: crouching hind legs gripped the front edge and extended a quarter of the way down toward the bottom of the pedestal. The cephalopod head was bent forward
column18: so that the ends of the facial feelers brushed the backs of huge fore paws which clasped the croucher’s elevated knees. The aspect of the whole was abnormally life-like
column19: and the more subtly fearful because its source was so totally unknown. Its vast
column20: awesome
column21: and incalculable age was unmistakable; yet not one link did it shew with any known type of art belonging to civilisation’s youth—or indeed to any other time. Totally separate and apart
column22: its very material was a mystery; for the soapy
column23: greenish-black stone with its golden or iridescent flecks and striations resembled nothing familiar to geology or mineralogy. The characters along the base were equally baffling; and no member present
column24: despite a representation of half the world’s expert learning in this field
column25: could form the least notion of even their remotest linguistic kinship. They
column27: belonged to something horribly remote and distinct from mankind as we know it; something frightfully suggestive of old and unhallowed cycles of life in which our world and our conceptions have no part.

column1: And yet
column2: as the members severally shook their heads and confessed defeat at the Inspector’s problem
column3: there was one man in that gathering who suspected a touch of bizarre familiarity in the monstrous shape and writing
column4: and who presently told with some diffidence of the odd trifle he knew. This person was the late William Channing Webb
column5: Professor of Anthropology in Princeton University
column6: and an explorer of no slight note. Professor Webb had been engaged
column7: forty-eight years before
column8: in a tour of Greenland and Iceland in search of some Runic inscriptions which he failed to unearth; and whilst high up on the West Greenland coast had encountered a singular tribe or cult of degenerate Esquimaux whose religion
column9: a curious form of devil-worship
column10: chilled him with its deliberate bloodthirstiness and repulsiveness. It was a faith of which other Esquimaux knew little
column11: and which they mentioned only with shudders
column12: saying that it had come down from horribly ancient aeons before ever the world was made. Besides nameless rites and human sacrifices there were certain queer hereditary rituals addressed to a supreme elder devil or tornasuk; and of this Professor Webb had taken a careful phonetic copy from an aged angekok or wizard-priest
column13: expressing the sounds in Roman letters as best he knew how. But just now of prime significance was the fetish which this cult had cherished
column14: and around which they danced when the aurora leaped high over the ice cliffs. It was
column15: the professor stated
column16: a very crude bas-relief of stone
column17: comprising a hideous picture and some cryptic writing. And so far as he could tell
column18: it was a rough parallel in all essential features of the bestial thing now lying before the meeting.

column1: This data
column2: received with suspense and astonishment by the assembled members
column3: proved doubly exciting to Inspector Legrasse; and he began at once to ply his informant with questions. Having noted and copied an oral ritual among the swamp cult-worshippers his men had arrested
column4: he besought the professor to remember as best he might the syllables taken down amongst the diabolist Esquimaux. There then followed an exhaustive comparison of details
column5: and a moment of really awed silence when both detective and scientist agreed on the virtual identity of the phrase common to two hellish rituals so many worlds of distance apart. What
column6: in substance
column7: both the Esquimau wizards and the Louisiana swamp-priests had chanted to their kindred idols was something very like this—the word-divisions being guessed at from traditional breaks in the phrase as chanted aloud:

column1: “Ph’nglui mglw’nafh Cthulhu R’lyeh wgah’nagl fhtagn.”
Legrasse had one point in advance of Professor Webb
column2: for several among his mongrel prisoners had repeated to him what older celebrants had told them the words meant. This text
column3: as given
column4: ran something like this:

column1: “In his house at R’lyeh dead Cthulhu waits dreaming.”
And now
column2: in response to a general and urgent demand
column3: Inspector Legrasse related as fully as possible his experience with the swamp worshippers; telling a story to which I could see my uncle attached profound significance. It savoured of the wildest dreams of myth-maker and theosophist
column4: and disclosed an astonishing degree of cosmic imagination among such half-castes and pariahs as might be least expected to possess it.

column1: On November 1st
column3: there had come to the New Orleans police a frantic summons from the swamp and lagoon country to the south. The squatters there
column4: mostly primitive but good-natured descendants of Lafitte’s men
column5: were in the grip of stark terror from an unknown thing which had stolen upon them in the night. It was voodoo
column6: apparently
column7: but voodoo of a more terrible sort than they had ever known; and some of their women and children had disappeared since the malevolent tom-tom had begun its incessant beating far within the black haunted woods where no dweller ventured. There were insane shouts and harrowing screams
column8: soul-chilling chants and dancing devil-flames; and
column9: the frightened messenger added
column10: the people could stand it no more.

column1: So a body of twenty police
column2: filling two carriages and an automobile
column3: had set out in the late afternoon with the shivering squatter as a guide. At the end of the passable road they alighted
column4: and for miles splashed on in silence through the terrible cypress woods where day never came. Ugly roots and malignant hanging nooses of Spanish moss beset them
column5: and now and then a pile of dank stones or fragment of a rotting wall intensified by its hint of morbid habitation a depression which every malformed tree and every fungous islet combined to create. At length the squatter settlement
column6: a miserable huddle of huts
column7: hove in sight; and hysterical dwellers ran out to cluster around the group of bobbing lanterns. The muffled beat of tom-toms was now faintly audible far
column8: far ahead; and a curdling shriek came at infrequent intervals when the wind shifted. A reddish glare
column9: too
column10: seemed to filter through the pale undergrowth beyond endless avenues of forest night. Reluctant even to be left alone again
column11: each one of the cowed squatters refused point-blank to advance another inch toward the scene of unholy worship
column12: so Inspector Legrasse and his nineteen colleagues plunged on unguided into black arcades of horror that none of them had ever trod before.

column1: The region now entered by the police was one of traditionally evil repute
column2: substantially unknown and untraversed by white men. There were legends of a hidden lake unglimpsed by mortal sight
column3: in which dwelt a huge
column4: formless white polypous thing with luminous eyes; and squatters whispered that bat-winged devils flew up out of caverns in inner earth to worship it at midnight. They said it had been there before D’Iberville
column5: before La Salle
column6: before the Indians
column7: and before even the wholesome beasts and birds of the woods. It was nightmare itself
column8: and to see it was to die. But it made men dream
column9: and so they knew enough to keep away. The present voodoo orgy was
column10: indeed
column11: on the merest fringe of this abhorred area
column12: but that location was bad enough; hence perhaps the very place of the worship had terrified the squatters more than the shocking sounds and incidents.

column1: Only poetry or madness could do justice to the noises heard by Legrasse’s men as they ploughed on through the black morass toward the red glare and the muffled tom-toms. There are vocal qualities peculiar to men
column2: and vocal qualities peculiar to beasts; and it is terrible to hear the one when the source should yield the other. Animal fury and orgiastic licence here whipped themselves to daemoniac heights by howls and squawking ecstasies that tore and reverberated through those nighted woods like pestilential tempests from the gulfs of hell. Now and then the less organised ululation would cease
column3: and from what seemed a well-drilled chorus of hoarse voices would rise in sing-song chant that hideous phrase or ritual:

column1: “Ph’nglui mglw’nafh Cthulhu R’lyeh wgah’nagl fhtagn.”
Then the men
column2: having reached a spot where the trees were thinner
column3: came suddenly in sight of the spectacle itself. Four of them reeled
column4: one fainted
column5: and two were shaken into a frantic cry which the mad cacophony of the orgy fortunately deadened. Legrasse dashed swamp water on the face of the fainting man
column6: and all stood trembling and nearly hypnotised with horror.

column1: In a natural glade of the swamp stood a grassy island of perhaps an acre’s extent
column2: clear of trees and tolerably dry. On this now leaped and twisted a more indescribable horde of human abnormality than any but a Sime or an Angarola could paint. Void of clothing
column3: this hybrid spawn were braying
column4: bellowing
column5: and writhing about a monstrous ring-shaped bonfire; in the centre of which
column6: revealed by occasional rifts in the curtain of flame
column7: stood a great granite monolith some eight feet in height; on top of which
column8: incongruous with its diminutiveness
column9: rested the noxious carven statuette. From a wide circle of ten scaffolds set up at regular intervals with the flame-girt monolith as a centre hung
column10: head downward
column11: the oddly marred bodies of the helpless squatters who had disappeared. It was inside this circle that the ring of worshippers jumped and roared
column12: the general direction of the mass motion being from left to right in endless Bacchanal between the ring of bodies and the ring of fire.

column1: It may have been only imagination and it may have been only echoes which induced one of the men
column3: to fancy he heard antiphonal responses to the ritual from some far and unillumined spot deeper within the wood of ancient legendry and horror. This man
column4: Joseph D. Galvez
column5: I later met and questioned; and he proved distractingly imaginative. He indeed went so far as to hint of the faint beating of great wings
column6: and of a glimpse of shining eyes and a mountainous white bulk beyond the remotest trees—but I suppose he had been hearing too much native superstition.

column1: Actually
column2: the horrified pause of the men was of comparatively brief duration. Duty came first; and although there must have been nearly a hundred mongrel celebrants in the throng
column3: the police relied on their firearms and plunged determinedly into the nauseous rout. For five minutes the resultant din and chaos were beyond description. Wild blows were struck
column4: shots were fired
column5: and escapes were made; but in the end Legrasse was able to count some forty-seven sullen prisoners
column6: whom he forced to dress in haste and fall into line between two rows of policemen. Five of the worshippers lay dead
column7: and two severely wounded ones were carried away on improvised stretchers by their fellow-prisoners. The image on the monolith
column8: of course
column9: was carefully removed and carried back by Legrasse.

column1: Examined at headquarters after a trip of intense strain and weariness
column2: the prisoners all proved to be men of a very low
column3: mixed-blooded
column4: and mentally aberrant type. Most were seamen
column5: and a sprinkling of negroes and mulattoes
column6: largely West Indians or Brava Portuguese from the Cape Verde Islands
column7: gave a colouring of voodooism to the heterogeneous cult. But before many questions were asked
column8: it became manifest that something far deeper and older than negro fetichism was involved. Degraded and ignorant as they were
column9: the creatures held with surprising consistency to the central idea of their loathsome faith.

column1: They worshipped
column3: the Great Old Ones who lived ages before there were any men
column4: and who came to the young world out of the sky. Those Old Ones were gone now
column5: inside the earth and under the sea; but their dead bodies had told their secrets in dreams to the first men
column6: who formed a cult which had never died. This was that cult
column7: and the prisoners said it had always existed and always would exist
column8: hidden in distant wastes and dark places all over the world until the time when the great priest Cthulhu
column9: from his dark house in the mighty city of R’lyeh under the waters
column10: should rise and bring the earth again beneath his sway. Some day he would call
column11: when the stars were ready
column12: and the secret cult would always be waiting to liberate him.

column1: Meanwhile no more must be told. There was a secret which even torture could not extract. Mankind was not absolutely alone among the conscious things of earth
column2: for shapes came out of the dark to visit the faithful few. But these were not the Great Old Ones. No man had ever seen the Old Ones. The carven idol was great Cthulhu
column3: but none might say whether or not the others were precisely like him. No one could read the old writing now
column4: but things were told by word of mouth. The chanted ritual was not the secret—that was never spoken aloud
column5: only whispered. The chant meant only this: “In his house at R’lyeh dead Cthulhu waits dreaming.”

column1: Only two of the prisoners were found sane enough to be hanged
column2: and the rest were committed to various institutions. All denied a part in the ritual murders
column3: and averred that the killing had been done by Black Winged Ones which had come to them from their immemorial meeting-place in the haunted wood. But of those mysterious allies no coherent account could ever be gained. What the police did extract
